Oṃ tat sat.
Now follows the recitation of the aphorisms (*sūtra*) from the *Śivasūtravārtika*. 1. In the first illumination (*prakāśa*).
1. Consciousness is the Self;
2. Knowledge is bondage;
3. The group of wombs is the body of kalās.
4. Mātṛkā is the locus of knowledge;
5. Bhairava is exertion;
6. In the union of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), there is the withdrawal of the universe.
7. In the distinction between waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, there is the consciousness of the enjoyment of the fourth state (turya).
8. Knowledge is the waking state;
9. Dreaming consists of mental constructs (vikalpa).
10. Non-discrimination is the illusory state of deep sleep;
11. The enjoyer of the triad is Vīreśa;
12. Amazement is the stages of yoga.
13. The maiden is the supreme power of will (*icchā-śakti*).
14. The visible world is the body.
15. Through the friction of the mind within the heart, there is the perception of the wild beasts of the visible world.
16. Or, from the unification with the pure reality (śuddhatattva); 17. the power of one's own state; 18. discursive investigation is self-knowledge.

19. The bliss of the world is the happiness of meditative absorption (samādhi). 20. Through the conjunction of the powers (śakti), the body arises. 21. The conjunction of the elements, the differentiation of the elements, and the union of the universe.
22. From the arising of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*), the attainment of the state of a Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśa*) occurs.
23. From the contemplation of the great lake (*mahāhrada*), there is the experience of the potency of mantra (*mantravīrya*).
Thus end the aphorisms of the First Light (*prathamaprakāśa*).
2. In the *Prakāśa*, 1: Mind is the mantra;
2: Effort is the practitioner.
3. The existence of the body of knowledge is the secret of mantra.
4. The expansion of consciousness within the womb is a specific dream of ignorance.
5. When knowledge arises spontaneously, that is the state of Śiva, the sky-farer (khecarī).
6. The Guru is the means; 7. The awakening to the wheel of the Mātṛkās;
8. The body is the oblation.
9. Knowledge is food.
10. In the withdrawal of knowledge, there is the perception of dreams arising from it. These are the aphorisms of the second chapter.
3. In the *Prakāśa*: 1. Self (*ātman*), mind (*citta*), 2.
Knowledge (*jñāna*), bondage (*bandha*).
3. Māyā is the non-discrimination of the principles (tattva) beginning with *kalā*.
4. The withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) of the *kalās* within the body.
5. The withdrawal of the channels (*nāḍī*), mastery over the elements (*bhūtajaya*), isolation from the elements (*bhūtakaivalya*), and the distinctness of the elements (*bhūtapṛthaktva*).
6. Accomplishment arises from the obscuration of delusion;
7. Through the conquest of delusion, there is the infinite enjoyment [of] the victory over innate gnosis;
8. One who possesses a second hand while awake.
The self is the dancer;
the inner self is the stage;
the senses are the spectators.
12. From the power of the intellect, the accomplishment of sentient beings [occurs].
13. The state of being independent is established.
14. As it is there, so it is elsewhere.
15. Due to the inherent nature of emission (*visarga*), because it does not exist externally, its persistence [is internal].
16. Focused attention on the seed-syllable (*bījāvadhāna*).
17. Seated upon the throne, one immerses oneself comfortably in the lake.
18. One brings about the manifestation of one's own measure.
19. With the destruction of ignorance comes the destruction of birth.
20. Within the *ka*-group and the others reside the Mothers of Beings, such as Māheśvarī and the rest.
21. The fourth [element] should be poured like oil upon the three.
22. Immersed in one's own mind, one should enter.
23. In the center, there is the production of the inferior.
24. Equal vision in the practice of the vital breath (prāṇa). 25. The rising again of what was lost through the non-connection of the measures (mātrā) with conviction.
26. One becomes equal to Śiva.
27. The observance is the maintenance of the body; 28. Recitation is discourse;
29. Giving is self-knowledge.
30. He who stands as the witness and is the cause of knowledge;
31. His own accumulation of powers is the universe; 32. [He is] both maintenance and dissolution.
33. Even when that [mind] is active, there is no cessation, because of the existence of the knower. 34. There is mentalization of pleasure and pain externally.
35. But one who is liberated from that is the Kevalin.

36. But the self whose nature is action is bound by delusion (moha). 37. When distinctions are set aside, there is the state of being the agent for another creation. 38. The power of the instrument [arises] from its own experience.
39. The vitalizing of the three steps and so forth; 40. Just as with the stability of the mind, [it occurs] within the body, the organs, and the external [world];
41. From desire, there is the outward movement of that which is bound externally.
Then, through the destruction of that cognition which has ascended [to that level], there is the destruction of the individual soul (jīva).
At that time, liberated from the sheath of the elements, he becomes supreme and equal to the Lord.
This is the natural connection with the vital breath (prāṇa).
45. By means of restraint (saṃyama) upon the middle of the interior of the nose—what [is gained] here? [The mastery of] the left, the right, and the Suṣumṇā.
46. There shall be a further closing [of the senses].
These are the aphorisms of the third chapter.
This recitation of the Sūtras for the Śivasūtravārtika is completed.
Now, a summary of the subjects expounded in the Sūtras within the Śivasūtravārtika;
therein, first, in the First Light (Prathama-prakāśa):
1. The proposition regarding the essential nature of the Self as consisting of knowledge and action.
2. The definition of the obscuration of the Self's essential nature, which has as its cause the manifestation of duality in the form of "I-ness" and "mine-ness."

3. An exposition of the powers that cause the loss of knowledge in the individual soul (aṇu). 4. An exposition of the manifestation of duality, its causal power, its locus, and so forth. 5. [The power] which effects the veiling of one's own nature, for the purpose of removing the aforementioned appearance of knowledge.

And there is the instruction on the cause for the sake of realizing one's own true nature (6). Furthermore, in the thorough knowledge of that true nature, there is the determination of the non-abandonment of the realization of non-duality, both externally and internally.
7. An exposition on the firmness of the perception of one's own true nature as being identical across states such as waking and others;
8. [The fact that] in all objective existents, it is the conscious self alone that exists in the form of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped.

The definition of the waking state, which consists of the power of knowledge whose nature is vibration (sphuraṇa). 9. The definition of the dreaming state, which consists of conceptual constructions (vikalpa) that delineate various obscuring objects for the bound soul (paśu).

10. Because the power of the essential nature of knowledge and the object of knowledge is unmanifested, it is characterized by the state of deep sleep brought forth by the power of *māyā*, which obscures its own true nature. 11. For one who is established in his own true nature, [this state] is on an equal footing with the three aforementioned states.
The designation "Lord of Heroes" (Vīreśvara) is due to his capacity for the creative play (*camatkṛti*) of the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth.

12. [This is] the explanation of the manifestation of self-perfection (*ātmasiddhi*), which consists in ascending to the unsurpassed stage (*anuttarabhūmikā*) through the complete stabilization of the contemplation of the conscious self (*cidātman*) flashing forth as the universal soul (*viśvātman*).
13. Thus is the description of the attainment of unimpeded sovereignty through immersion in the nature of consciousness free from obscuration for one who has ascended to the higher planes.
14. For this very [yogi], by virtue of the realization of identity with the universe...

15. The description of pervasiveness both internally and externally; the determination of the true nature of all entities through the dissolution of all latent impressions (vāsanās) in the heart, which serves as the substratum for the object, the subject, and so forth.
16. Exposition of the means for attaining the consciousness of Śiva as proclaimed; 17. Exposition of the means for attaining the consciousness of Śakti;
18. Description of the realization of one's own consciousness.
19. An exposition of the bliss of samādhi, which brings forth an excellence of bliss consisting of the self-luminous vibration [of consciousness] both externally and internally.
20. Of such a perfected yogin, through the immersion into the nature of unobscured consciousness...

21. The demonstration of unimpeded sovereignty in manifesting desired bodies and so forth; 22. The description of the attainment of the splendor of playing and creating at will through the perfection of this very sovereignty.
22. Following the indifference toward limited accomplishments, the description of the attainment of one's own imperial sovereignty.

23. The description of the possession of great vitality resulting from the cultivation of the reflective awareness of the nature of consciousness, which consists of the powers of the possessor of power—the cause for the arising of all phenomena.
Thus ends the first chapter. 1.
Now, in the second chapter:
1. The designation of the very mind whose nature is auspicious through qualities such as omniscience as being the mantra;
2. The exposition of the means for the immersion (*samāveśa*) into the mantra whose nature is the mind.
3. An exposition on the secret nature of the mantra within the science of self-knowledge (*ātma-vidyā*), which consists of the expansion of self-luminosity.
4. When the mind’s natural qualities (*prākṛta-guṇa*) are dissolved, there is the means for ascending to the unsurpassed state (*anuttara-pada*);
otherwise, through the emergence of impure knowledge (*aśuddha-vidyā*), various delusions arise.
Section 5: An Exposition on the Attainment of Moving within the Space of Consciousness of One’s Own Self through the Arising of Pure Knowledge (vidyā) from the Light of One’s Own Self.

6. [This is] the demonstration of the means [to liberation], beginning with the power of the mantras and so forth as proclaimed, through the attainment of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) by recourse to a true guru.
7. Through the descent of power by taking refuge in a true guru and so forth, [there arises] the fruit consisting of the knowledge of the true path.

Lānuśāsana 8: Thus, when the fire of blazing gnosis— characterized by identity with the mantra— is present, for the sake of non-rebirth, [one acts] toward the body which has as its material cause the karmic impurity that is the cause of rebirth.
9. The description of [the offering] as the oblation (havis):
the extension of the knowledge that brings about the supreme satisfaction of the yogin who has attained the glory of his own Self, [to the status of] the sacrificial substance to be consumed.

10. In the withdrawal of undifferentiated knowledge (*aviśiṣṭavidyā-saṃhāra*), because one contemplates the entities arising from the conceptualizations based on their prior states as being like a dream— by virtue of their existence as the dawning of self-luminosity— and because of the constant satisfaction consisting in the mental construction of one's own light;
The second chapter is "Instruction on That.
Now, in the third chapter:

In this section on sovereign power (*vibhūti*), which is intended [to be explained] by means of the manifestation of one's own nature (*svarūpa*) and so forth, there is first of all the definition of the mind (*citta*) associated with the atom (*aṇu*) as the Self (*ātman*), characterized by qualities such as volition (*saṃkalpa*) and reflection (*manana*).
2. An exposition on how unreal cognition acts as a bond because the mind is distracted by its attachment to objects such as passion;
3. [This occurs] due to *māyā*, which consists in the absence of the realization of the true nature of reality (*tattva*).

The description of one's own nature (4): Through the firmness of meditating on the dissolution of the parts of the body— which is composed of a collection of principles— into their respective causes, one attains the true nature of one's own self.
5. An exposition on the attainment of the body which is the self of supreme awakening, the fruit of the individual means (āṇavopāya).

Even for this body composed of the elements beginning with earth, through the proficiency gained by the practice of *dhāraṇā* upon each respective element, there arises the stability of those respective elements and elemental derivatives.

6. An examination of the autonomy [of the yogin] regarding the transference [of consciousness], the creation [of bodies], the joining together, the separating apart, and so forth, due to the proficiency gained from retaining the aforementioned principles and so on; [and how] for the yogin, there is no obscuration caused by delusion.

An exposition on the desire for the attainment of the enjoyment of each respective reality (tattva), and the acceptance of the attainment of omniscience and other powers through the contemplation of one's former pure state when that [desire] is otherwise.

7. Through the pacification of the delusion of the self—which consists of the pervasive misconception [of reality] due to its infinite extent—there is the description of the arising of pure *vidyā*, which is self-luminous, for one who is perfectly awakened. 8. Thus, by virtue of having attained innate *vidyā*, the universe is like one's own radiance.
9. A description of the final consummation for one who perceives through the state of constant awakening;
[and] the self’s mastery over the dramatic play of the world as it acts at will through immersion in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of each respective entity within the universe.

Section 10: The designation of the *puryaṣṭaka* as the stage for the dramatic play of the world— consisting of its activity, maintenance, and so forth, with the aforementioned qualities as its essence and the Self (*ātman*) as the performer— is now explained.
11. Precisely because of this state of perfect awakening, there is the mention [of the Self] as the spectator of the dramatic play of the world, whose senses are under its own control.
12. Due to the existence of the intellect (*buddhi*) which determines the nature of pure consciousness, there is supreme excellence.
The Teaching 13. The demonstration that the Self, possessing the aforementioned qualities, is endowed with the perfection of independence 14.
[This applies] even to the bodies of others upon which [the Lord] presides, just as it does to the body He Himself inhabits.
[2-1 4] An exposition on the manifestation of qualities such as omniscience and sovereignty;
and an exposition on how this one, who is independent through powers such as entering the bodies of others, does not suffer the loss or non-attainment of his own abode.

16. It is taught that for one who is concentrated through the constant practice of the self-reflection of consciousness (*vid-ātma-vimarśana*) within the state of Śakti, the cause of not falling away from one's own abode is precisely that very state of concentration.
17. From the attainment of immersion into the state of Śakti, there arises the ease of accessing the supreme nature.

The Vision (darśana) 18: The capacity for the accomplishment of unprecedented realities, which manifests the sovereign power of the abode [of consciousness] through the cultivation of the two means consisting of focused attention upon what has been taught and entry [into that state].

19. An investigation of the one who is to be led. 20. Instruction on the fruit consisting of non-rebirth resulting from the emergence of Pure Knowledge through the cultivation of the aforementioned means.

20. Even for an atom that has attained perfection, due to a lapse in attentiveness caused by the interpenetration of sound (śabdānuvedhana), there is a description of the delusive nature of the powers (mātṛkā-śakti) known as Ghorā and others, beginning with Āheśvarī.

21. It has been stated that among the various types of Mothers (mātṛbhedas), there is a description of the state of constant meditative absorption (*nityasamāhitatā*) through the practice of cultivating firmness in the contemplation of the pure Śiva-principle (*śuddhaśivatattva*), by means of the solidification of the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*).
22. An exposition of the means for attaining firmness in the realization of the pure Śiva-principle, which arises from penetrating the phonemes (varṇa).
23. [This occurs] because of the abandonment of the reflective awareness (vimarśa) regarding the states at the initial and final limits of the phonemes, and through the middle limit—
24. In the state of rest (*viśrama*), because of the initial onset of various conceptual constructions (*vikalpanā*) and so forth, there is the determination of the attainment of delusion (*moha*).

In the absorption (*samāpatti*) of the self-luminosity of the Supreme Sound (*paranāda*), through the firmness of experiencing the non-duality of the words, mantras, and so forth—which emanate from the Supreme (*parā*) down to the level of *vaikharī*—the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*) [is realized].

The determination of the attainment of capacity: [25] through the continuous contemplation of the collection of principles beginning with Māyā, by means of attaining the power of entry into each respective stage (*bhūmi*),
there arises the state of omniscience which animates the body of the [practitioner] whose [limited] states of being have perished.
26. An exposition on the attainment of supreme sovereignty, such as being the creator of all;
thus, an exposition on the state of being identical in form to Śiva, even while the body and other factors persist, due to the excellence of the constant contemplation of the true nature of Śiva.
27. Thus, for one who possesses steady concentration, even the activity of the body is extended [to be considered] as a vow.
28. In that same way, for one who has ascended to the state of the object of the contemplation of the supreme *ahaṃbhāva* (I-consciousness) which is connected [to it]—
29. Even ordinary conversation is defined as *japa* (repetition of mantras).
The extension [of this principle] is that for those bound by animal-like ignorance (*paśu*), the manifestation of the knowledge of one's own true nature is treated as a gift.

30. An exposition of the bestowing of liberation and other qualities, such as the capacity for the manifestation of the universe and the enjoyment of the manifold forms [of the Lord], belonging to the yogi who has attained the aforementioned perfection.

31. The description of the manifestation [of the Self] as the universal soul, consisting of its own unsurpassed power, through the attainment of identity with Śiva. 32. Through the realization of being the universal soul, by one's own will, the universe is manifested by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*).
33. An exposition on the agency of maintenance and dissolution.
34. An instruction on how [the Self] remains with its own essential nature undiminished even during the times of creation, maintenance, and destruction.
[The experience of] various kinds of internal and external pleasure and pain through the non-deviation from one's own self-reflection...
Even during manifestation, there is the description of non-contact with that [object];
35. the statement that [the subject] rests solely in pure consciousness by virtue of its own self-manifestation being undiminished, even while remaining untouched by pleasure and the like.

36. Through the manifestation of the ego-sense (*ahaṃbhāva*) toward the body and so forth, and due to the impact of delusion regarding pleasure and other states, there is the definition of the bondage of action (*karma*), the self (*ātman*), and the state of being a bound soul (*saṃsāripaśutva*).
37. [This occurs] for one who does not reflect upon anything whatsoever as distinct from oneself.

38. An exposition on the attainment of the power of being the creator of unprecedented creations, variegated by the arrangement of ever-new manifestations, through the restoration to one's own essential nature; [and] the capacity for the production of other creations whose nature is the blossoming of diverse states of being.
The instruction on the cause of one's own direct experience (svānubhava) [is given] in verse 39;
it is the teaching on the primary cause for the transfer of the power of entities into the fourth state (turyāvasthā), which is the principal among states such as waking and so forth.

40. Because the mind does not deviate from its own nature, even when the collection of organs is present, there is the description of the manifestation of the nature of consciousness through the unfolding of that very nature.
41. [This occurs] for the Self who, while in a lower state, desires the engagement in seeing, hearing, and so forth.

The description of the engagement with objects such as sound and touch arises from the impelling of the external wheel of instruments by the desire for the infusion of the power of consciousness into the organs of cognition and action.

42. Through the empowerment of one's own strength and effort, for one whose consciousness has become firmly established, there arises the teaching on the pacification of the eightfold subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) of the external self, due to the abandonment of the desire for bondage.
43. Upon the destruction of the impurity consisting of desire, [there is the attainment] of the ground of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth.
The praise of one who has become established [in Śiva] as being equal to Śiva due to the existence of the connection with the elemental body (44).
Because of being grounded in self-luminous consciousness, even when the identification with the *puryaṣṭaka* has subsided...

45. [This is] the description of the state of remaining within the sheaths of the vital breath and its associated elements due to one's natural constitution, for as long as there is the experience of karma. [This is] for the purpose of practicing the realization of one’s own unsurpassed Self in order to attain equality with Śiva.
46. The instruction on the worship of the Unstruck Sound-Brahman (Anāhata-Śabda-Brahman), which is the Self of the vital breath (Prāṇātman).

[And] the realization of one's own Self through the destruction of impurities by means of the path of the aforementioned instruction for the All-pervading Lord, who—though established in the non-differentiation [of reality]—is [perceived as such] due to the power of Māyā.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Teaching on the Acceptance of Śiva-nature as Complete and Solid Bliss. || 3 ||
And thus concludes the summary of the subject matter of the aphorisms of the *Śivasūtravārtika*.
Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Śambhu, whose body is the manifestation of the bliss of one's own Self.
Now,
the Śiva Sūtras.
Accompanied by the Vārttika composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭa Bhāskarācārya. Therein, this is the first chapter.
Page 1.

Bow down to the God who grants boons, the beloved of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, whose crest-jewel is the crescent moon, and who is the agent of the creation and dissolution of the world; he who is beautiful through the power of his own sovereignty manifested from the most translucent, unsurpassed, and eternal state.
The Lord, whose primary ornament is the digit known as Amā which revives the universe;

who is habituated to performing the fivefold cosmic acts such as creation and so forth; whose true nature consists of luminosity and other qualities; and who is intent on the sport of manifesting the universe and other such activities.
The meaning is that he has entered his own self, which bestows boons upon its own self through the attainment of its most excellent nature;

the external meaning, however, is clear. Here, in the first quarter [of the verse], there is the general nature of consciousness (*sāmānyacitsvarūpa*) as being primarily the nature of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), while in the second...

By emphasizing the predominance of the essential nature of Śakti in the arising of innate knowledge (sahajavidyā), and by describing the manifestation of power (vibhūti) primarily as the splendor of the cosmic play (viśvanāṭya) in what remains,
the introduction to the three lights (prakāśatraya) to be explained hereafter has been made. || 1-1 ||

Salutation to Śiva, whose nature is concealed by the radiance of his own eternally arisen self-luminosity, and whose body is the form of the one, perfectly full consciousness. [To him who is ever-arisen and self-manifesting...]

The manifestation of the contracted individual soul (*aṇu*) occurs through the obscuration of Śiva— whose form is enveloped by a constant, outward-flowing radiance consisting of His own non-differentiated, surging, and most vivid manifestations as blue and other colors—
even though, in reality, He remains the full density of Being-Consciousness. Although that [full state] exists, it is not [manifest].
"Pahāniḥ" (abandonment) is the intended meaning; by this, the entire essence of what will be explained regarding the commencement, practice, and so forth in the third chapter is indicated.
This lineage of the gurus, which is observed in a particular manuscript—

As for the intended meaning: just as one's very own self is Śiva, so too it will be established [later] that "therein, within the self alone, the state of Śiva (śivatā) of everything is indeed entirely unbroken. Now, how can there be the state of Śiva for those who are transmigratory beings? To this it is said: by virtue of the power of delusion.
This [consciousness] is as if covered, but it is not actually covered in the ultimate sense, because it is always manifest; for if it were covered, all worldly activity would cease,
and so it will be stated later.
"And that [reality] is veiled by the semblance of cognition such as 'I-ness,' 'this-ness,' and so forth.
What, then, is the cause for its removal? It is precisely the grace of the Lord (Īśvara). And thus it is said:
"O Goddess, by the power of the descent of grace (śaktipāta), one is led toward a true Guru."

Thus, when there is grace (*anugraha*) in that regard, his own nature, described in the aforementioned manner, will become manifest. Furthermore, for one of such a kind, everything occurs under his own control. This will be stated [later]:
"Śiva is directly one's own nature."
And so forth. || 1–2 ||
Formerly, on the glorious Mahādeva mountain, the Śiva-sūtras indeed appeared to that teacher Vasugupta by virtue of a perfected one's (siddha) command. 1.3.
He, in turn, gave it along with its secret [commentary] to the venerable Bhaṭṭa Sūra;
he likewise gave those four sections to the venerable Kallaṭa.
Then, he explained these three [chapters] to them by means of his own *Spanda-sūtras*,
along with the final section (*khaṇḍa*) via the commentary titled *Tattvārthacintāmaṇi*. (From the Commentary, page 3)
[This is] called a "fragment" (khaṇḍa). || 1-5 ||
In this way, he also spoke of this secret to his maternal cousin,
the illustrious Pradyumna Bhaṭṭa, and he [Pradyumna] in turn to his own son.
He gave it to the illustrious one named Prajñārjuna, who spoke thus;
and he, in turn, gave it to his own disciple, the illustrious Mahādevabhaṭṭa.
He bestowed it upon his own son, the illustrious Śrīkaṇṭhabhaṭṭa;
having received it from him, I now compose this Sūtravārtika with reverence.
I am Bhāskara, the one who acts for the sake of the gods, impelled by the assembly of my disciples;
[I act] because, due to the confusion of the scriptures, their intellects have been led astray by error. (1.9)
Therefore, for the sake of those who are delicate, I shall explain those sūtras:
"In that regard, the state of Śiva is entirely unfragmented within the Self alone; the Self itself is Śiva."

The conscious self (*cidātmā*) is not, however, something separate as it is conceived by other philosophical schools; for the state of Śiva (*śivatā*)— which is established by one's own direct experience, which is the locus of the sovereignty consisting of a perfect and supramundane relationship of cause and effect, and which is the resting place of all things— is that which is to be recognized at every moment.

In the state of empirical transaction (*vyavahāra*), the sovereignty over the acts of creating and manifesting entities exists within the individual atoms of consciousness (*cidaṇu*) as a characteristic that is perceivable only by those with refined aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*). That very [sovereignty], through the power of subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) manifested by its own will (*svecchā*) via *māyā*,
appears to the *pudgala*s as if it were veiled by the ignorance of "this-ness" (*idantā-jñāna*).

Since it cannot be attained [by other means], the descent of the Sūtras has occurred from Śrī Śiva—who, desiring to show grace toward those people worthy of favor, intends to make that [reality] known—verily so. 1-10.
She is always veiled by the appearance of cognitions such as "I" and "this," and so forth;
for the sake of destroying that veil and for the sake of realizing her own true nature, Śiva [acts]. (1.11)

Overwhelmed by compassion, he spoke the Sūtras preceded by the knowledge of *saṃkrāma*—[those for those who have received] the most intense descent of power (*tīvratara-śaktipāta*) through Śāmbhava-knowledge;
those favored by the medium-intense power (*tīvramadhya-śakti*) through Śākta-knowledge; and those possessing a mild descent of power (*manda-śaktipāta*).

By means of individual knowledge (*āṇavajñāna*), through the process of ascending the rungs of the ladder that is progressively higher and higher, they attain the state that is supreme above all; therefore, with respect to those who possess the requisite qualification (*adhikārin*), the aphorisms are presented in their proper sequence.
Śiva is directly his own essential nature; from its unfolding (*unmeṣa*) and closing (*nimeṣa*)— where "unfolding" is the expansion of power (*śakti*) and "closing" is its contraction—
arise the wheel of the powers (*kalācakra*) such as consciousness (*cit*), will (*icchā*), and so forth, which constitute the universe whose sole form is pure, stainless consciousness.
The emission and maintenance consist either of the pentad of principles beginning with Śiva, which has that [consciousness] as its cause, or of the expansion of powers such as Khecarī. || 1-12 ||
The emergence and dissolution of the world, of the body of knowledge, and of the wheel of kalās are bound to the expansion and contraction of the flow of power (śakti). (1.13)
Regarding the presentation of its essential nature (*tatsvarūpa-upanyāsa*),
there are many conflicting views (*vipratipattayaḥ*)— that is, the disputants hold differing opinions due to the varying degrees of their obscuration by impurity (*mala-pratibandha-tāratamya*).
Among these, the worldly folk (*laukikāḥ*) [hold that] the body qualified by consciousness [is the self], while the Naiyāyikas...

The Mīmāṃsakas [regard it as] possessing qualities such as knowledge and consisting primarily of the principle of intellect (buddhi-tattva); the Buddhists [regard it as] the stream of consciousness (jñāna-saṃtāna); certain knowers of the Vedas [regard it as] the Void (śūnya), whose nature is non-existent Brahman; and the Mādhyamikas likewise hold this view.

The Pāñcarātras [regard] the Unmanifest; the Sāṃkhyas, the state of the "pure knowledge" (vijñānakalā); certain knowers of the Veda, the principle of Īśvara; the Grammarians, the principle of Sadāśiva;
and those who follow the Trika and other systems, the Self whose nature consists of transcending the universe and becoming identical with it.
They proceed [in this manner]. All these [beings], deprived of ultimate sovereignty by *māyā*, have fallen into the plane of duality.
For the purpose of dispelling that [state], Śiva composed the *Sūtra*—[known as the *Śivasūtra*].
He composed the Śivasūtras. || 1-14 ||
The Self is consciousness. 1-1.
Consciousness is established as the nature of the Self, consisting of knowledge and action;
since its nature is unobscured, by whom can its state of Śiva-hood be prevented? (1.15)
Regarding that concealment, Maheśvara states the aphorism for its presentation:
"Knowledge is bondage" (1.2).
That knowledge which consists of the manifestation of duality, in the form of "I" and "this is mine," is [false] knowledge. (1-16)
That which arises from the interpenetration of sound has its root in the impurity of Māyā (or, according to the *kh* manuscript,
is preceded by the impurity of Māyā). [This occurs] through the power of His own Māyā, which brings about the impossible for the Supreme Lord Himself, whose nature is eternally all-pervasive.

For the purpose of manifesting the drama of the universal self, like an actor who conceals his own sovereignty through a costume and assumes a state of limitation, he occupies the role of an atomic soul; because he conforms to the presence and absence of light, he is afflicted by the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence.

One's own self, in relation to external entities, consists of a cognition characterized by distinct and diverse manifestations through the established linguistic associations of "I" and "mine"; this very cognition constitutes the bondage known as the *āṇavamala*, which is defined by the obscuration of one's innate sovereignty.
The meaning is that the impurity consisting of illusion (māyīya-mala) has been described; its bondage is fully explained as being characterized by the veil of ignorance (avidyā-āvṛti). || 1-17 ||
But what cause did he state for this interpenetration by sound (or: for this [state] called the ignorance of sound)?
The Sūtra is the expounder of the "cords" (kalās), which are the deluders of the bound soul (paśu).
The group of sources (yonivarga) is the body of the arts (kalā). || 1-3 ||
The four sources (*yoni*) and powers (*śakti*) should be known as the cause of all:
Ambā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, and Vāmā; these are the forms of Śiva. (1-19)
The group or collection of these constitutes that body within the arts (kalās).
Those arts consist of the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa', and they are the cause of sound.
The Mothers, the Śaktis, the goddesses, the rays, and the Kalās are so designated; through the penetration of sound, these illuminate the cognition of the bound soul (paśu). 1-21.

Therefore, he becomes an object of enjoyment for them, because his own power (*vibhava*) is perpetually eclipsed by the flash of knowledge (*jñānābhāsa*) arising from them. [Since all powers originate from the fourfold power, the wheel of phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* arises from those very four powers; that indeed is the wheel of powers.]

The gross [level] consists of phonemes (*varṇa*), which, through the composition of words and sentences, transform into the form of all various worldly and transcendental sounds; this generates cognition in bound souls (*paśu*), by which they, having their power eclipsed, fall into the state of being objects of enjoyment for that [cognition]. Thus begins the section starting with "the sources" (*yonayaḥ*).
The intended meaning of the four verses [is as follows]. || 1-22 ||
Since it must be asked what the support for the appearance of knowledge and for those [energies] is, he therefore said:
"The support of knowledge is Mātṛkā. (1.4)
Of knowledge itself, which possesses two forms, there is a distinction between the higher and the lower. || 1-23 ||

The substratum and the support would be the single power Mātṛkā; through the manifestation of both non-dual appearance and duality, there is the nature of the two types of knowledge, namely the supreme (parā) and the intermediate (aparā).

The power that presides over both these types [of knowledge] is indeed the Universal Mother (Viśvajananī). Among them, in the case of supreme knowledge, it is the power called Aghorā, because it causes the manifestation of internal and external reality as being identical with one's own self.
In the other [inferior knowledge], due to the absence of the contemplation of non-duality, it produces an orientation toward the external.
The power called Ghora is that which completely veils the state of Śiva. || 1-4 ||
Thus, for the sake of the complete cessation of that knowledge which consists of obscuration— || 1-24 ||
To reveal His own essential nature, the Lord spoke this aphorism:
"Bhairava is effort" (1.5).
Thus, of Śiva, whose nature is consciousness and who is complete in his own essence. || 1-25 ||
The state of one desiring to manifest toward an effect without abandoning one's own essential nature is defined as *bhāva*, exertion (*udyoga*), unfolding (*unmeṣa*), and effort (*udyama*). (1.26)
That very [reality] is called the world, the principle of Śarva, and Bhairava;
even therein, within the throbbing radiance of its own spontaneous vibration, it is Bhairava. (1.27)
It is called "Bharaṇa" (sustaining), "Ramaṇa" (delighting), and "Vamana" (vomiting) because of these;
it is also so called because of the expansion of the undivided self-manifestation of the all-pervasive Consciousness. [In this context, the Śāmbhavopāya is intended.]

By the power of the City, for those people whose hearts have been purified by an exceedingly intense descent of the Supreme Power (para-śaktipāta) and who are fit for grace through such means as beholding the Siddhas and consuming [the sacramental substances] like carva, there occurs— without dependence on the constraints of performing recitation (japa), meditation (dhyāna), and so forth— the process consisting of filling, churning, and vomiting.

For those possessed by the supreme Bhairava, through the relishing of the continuous outpouring of the nectar of Śakti— which consists of the ever-expanding flow of knowledge and action— there arises once again the recovery of immersion into one's own essential nature, characterized by the tasting of ever-new nectar-flavors. Thus it is for those who have exerted themselves.
When one's own nature unfolds, the absence of obscuration to the light of consciousness is indeed established. || 1-28 ||

Thus, for this Bhairava-natured one whose body is consciousness and who is ever-striving, even during the unfolding [of manifestation], the luminosity of his own essential nature is not lost (or: is perceived; or: is dissolved).
Having said this, Maheśvara uttered the aphorism for the sake of establishing that state in which one's own stability does not diminish even for the duration of a moment. (1.30)
In the conjunction of the wheel of powers (śakticakra), there is the dissolution of the universe.
The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) constitute the entire universe, and they consist of knowledge and action;
these are the functions (*vṛttayaḥ*) previously described, and that is called the wheel (*cakra*) because of its revolving (*cakana*).
"Because of eating. (1-31)
The reintegration of that [universe] is its appropriation within one's own self in an instant;
it is withdrawal, a state of dissolution, and by that means, its [the universe's] attainment of the state of Śiva. (1.32)

Thus, when the unfolding of knowledge regarding sound, meaning, form, and so forth occurs, the cause is none other than the Supreme Self, Bhairava, who is Śiva; for at that time, the universe— which consists of the powers of knowledge and action— is non-different from his nature as the Absolute (Anuttara), which is the essence of light and self-awareness.
Upon grasping [the object], there occurs a dissolution consisting of its becoming one with the fire of Śiva, which is composed of supreme consciousness;

thus, even in the state of the closing of the eyes (*nimeṣa*), the self-abiding nature of the effect—which exists within the cause in an undivided manner—is not obscured. This is the intended meaning. || 1-33 ||
For the conscious Self, which does not fall away from the vibration of its own essential nature,
this distinction of waking and so forth is non-obstructive;
for that purpose, the Lord of Gods has here stated the aphorism according to the truth.
In the distinction between waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, consciousness is the expansion of the Fourth State (*turya*).

"The arising of the expansion of the Fourth. || 1-7 ||
The fourth state (turya) is said to be the reflective awareness of the absolute unity of one's own true nature. (1.35)

Because it is the nature that permeates everything and because its state is free from delusion, that consciousness known as the expansion of the Fourth (turyābhoga) is indeed the very nature of the perceiver. (1.36)
Even while clearly moving through the distinctions of waking and so forth, she remains steadfast; for by means of dreaming,
states such as memory and so on are grasped, and by means of deep sleep, states such as intoxication and fainting are grasped— thus, within these three states, there are other states.
Since these have already been explained among the *kṣepiṇīs*, there is no need for a separate explanation of them. Thus,

when the threefold activity of these [powers] unfolds in distinct operations, for the awakened yogin who reflects upon his own nature as a single, dense mass, the ultimate reality produced by these three states— [The rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source text.]
There is no such thing as "samāvṁti" (concealment); therefore, the effort of practicing meditative absorption (*samādhi*) is useless for him,
because it is improper to enjoin attention toward that which is already of a perfect nature, whereas in the case of that which is incomplete,
attention directed toward a limited object would contradict the attainment of perfection.
Such is the intended meaning of the two verses beginning with "in its own nature" (svasvarūpe). || 1-7 ||
Having spoken thus, the Supreme Lord [proceeded] for the manifestation of the waking state and the others.
He taught three Sūtras for the sake of establishing liberation while living: "Knowledge is the waking state. (1.8)
Buddhist, prideful, and conceptual; verbal, tactile, and born of form. (1.38)

Furthermore, whatever other sensory cognition there is—whether born of taste or born of smell—in this regard, the nature of the conscious self (cidātman) consists of the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped. (1.39)
The power of knowledge indeed vibrates; it is precisely here that it functions as the waking state.

For the bound soul (paśu), that very function is described as the loss of its true nature, consisting of determination, ego-inflation, volition, verbalization, touching, seeing, tasting, and smelling.

The meaning is as follows: knowledge consisting of the feet arises from the functioning of the external senses; the waking state, conditioned by adjuncts such as the "seer" (draṣṭṛ) and so forth, acts as an obscuration to one's own self for bound souls (paśus), whereas for the Lords (patis), it bestows the manifestation of their true nature. || 40 ||
Dreams are conceptual constructions. 1-9.
The constant arising of new and new conceptual constructions within the pervasive nature of vision is traditionally called "dream," because of the negation of external objects;
for when there is an absence of external objects, those [constructions] likewise subside.

Dream is the continuous emergence of ever-new conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that, independent of external objects, appear within with a variety of delineations such as cities, mountains, forests, and groves, and which perform their own specific causal functions.
The meaning is that it conceals the true nature of the bound soul (paśu). || 1-41 ||
Furthermore, the firmness or lack of firmness of conceptual constructions arises from their repeated manifestation;
that very state is to be known as the obscuration of the Lord, whose nature is power, due to his condition as a bound soul (paśu). (1.42)
Non-discrimination is the state of deep sleep characterized by illusion. || 1.10 ||

When there is no emergence of the power whose nature consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge, that constitutes the non-discrimination of the conscious form; this very state arises from a lack of reflective awareness (avimarśa). (1.43)
That very state is proclaimed as such because it nourishes the web of the veil of māyā;
when the recollection of objects is established within one's own self in the form of consciousness, that is deep sleep. (1.44)
Thus, through the Lord’s own repose, [the state] takes the form of the concealment of the bound soul (paśu).
In this way, there are three [types of obscuration], each of which is threefold through their mutual conjunction. (1.45)
The distinctions between the primary and the secondary aspects of the conscious self (cidātman) should be correctly understood.
Thus, in these two stages, the Lord consists of both knowledge and the object of knowledge.

In deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and in the fourth state (*turya*), however, the all-pervasive Lord is remembered as consisting of consciousness alone. In both these states, due to the cessation of the power that manifests as the nature of the object and the subject of cognition—just as the sun’s rays are withdrawn—the Self, whose nature is consciousness, does not manifest; this non-manifestation consists of a web of veils (*āvaraṇa*).
Deep sleep is of the nature of *māyā*, wherein both the object and its memory reside solely within the immediate, undivided Self;

yet it is not that even this [Self] is non-existent, because for one who has emerged from that state, the recollection of the blissful sleep and the lack of cognition would otherwise be impossible. Thus, in these three states, [the relationship between] the Lord (*pati*) and the bound soul (*paśu*) [is as follows].
The intention of the series of verses beginning with "jñāna" is that the non-manifestation of the manifestation of one's own nature is established by its very essence.
Now, these three states possess the three qualities (guṇas). || 1.47 ||
Having established that very point as a consequence, he stated the sūtra for that purpose:
"The Lord of Heroes is the enjoyer of the triad. (1.11)
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—this triad is designated as the qualities (guṇas).

For that [impurity] indeed arises sufficiently from its own essential nature in accordance with the [individual's] state; it is the veil for bound souls (paśu), but for the Lord who abides in His own nature, it does not exist. (1.49)
Because it is the form that permeates everything, it does not conceal its own nature;
in this very way, the body of consciousness is the source of the flow and outpourings of the fluctuations of the qualities (guṇas).
He is called the "enjoyer" (*bhoktā*) because of his appropriation [of objects], and he is called the "Lord" (*vibhu*) because of the pervasiveness of his expansion.

For this very reason, he is the Lord of Heroes (*vīreśa*), due to his state of being solely self-luminous. [This occurs] because of the predominance of each of the qualities (*guṇa*)—such as *sattva* and the rest—which arise from the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*), whose essence is the state of equilibrium among the qualities.

The meaning is that he is called Vīreśa because he is the agent of wonder (*camatkartṛ*) through the expansion of his own sovereign power (*svavaibhavaprasaraṇa*), consisting of the three states beginning with waking— namely, illumination (*prakāśa*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and delusion (*moha*). Thus,
the collection of rays arises from the three qualities (*guṇatraya*).
In this world of manifold possibilities, he is intent upon vomiting and swallowing.
Because he consumes [all things] even there, he is remembered as Vīreśvara.
Thus, such is his state even during emergence from his own essential nature. (1.53)
His own [nature] does not fall away; for that purpose, he taught the Sūtra:
"The stages of yoga are a source of wonder. (1-12)
Thus, the Lord whose nature is consciousness is the cause of all creation and so forth.
Beholding this entire world as being presided over by that very [Brahman], he who remains as if filled with wonder is truly possessed of intuitive insight. (1.55)
From his connection with the flood of states beginning with the *bindu*, there arises a sense of wonder;

those which are these stages of yoga (*yogabhūmi*) are the manifestations of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), because of the true state of immersion into one's own self as a mass of consciousness while savoring the essence of the nectar of the multitude of objects to be known.

For this yogin who perceives his own innate glory— which is eternally manifest and ever-expanding— through blossoming, unartificial means, there arises a state of wonderment at the sight of a previously unknown, supramundane, and astonishing reality,
occurring entirely without the need for practices such as focusing on the *bindu* or other specific locations.

That [state] arises as the indicator of having ascended to the level of the supreme reality (paratattva), because of its connection with the flood of states beginning with the Bindu; the ablative case is used here due to the elision of a word ending in a lyap suffix (i.e., it is understood as "having departed from" the Bindu, etc.). || 1-56 ||
Thus, all her desires unfold without obstruction;
for that purpose, the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara spoke this sūtra.
The maiden Umā is the supreme power of will. || 1-13 ||
The power that transcends all is the will (*icchā*) of the Supreme Self alone;
through its union with universal seeing and agency, it brings about the creation and destruction [of the world], like a mother. (1.58)
Therefore, through immersion into the nature of unobstructed consciousness,

that very state becomes the cause for the omnipresent Lord everywhere; indeed, it is solely through union with His will-power (*icchā-śakti*), which contains all powers within its womb, that He exists everywhere throughout this visible world.
Unobstructed sovereignty exists, such that however He wills, so does He manifest.

The meaning is that by this, the entire universe—from the unconditioned (anāśrita) down to the earth—shines forth as if it were His own limb, in the form of a dense mass of unobscured consciousness. || 1-59 ||
"In this way, for this [Self] which consists of all things, is there one body like that of an embodied being, or is it everything? Regarding this, the Lord of the Gods spoke: (1.60)
The visible is the body. || 1-14 ||
For this source of all existence, Supreme Śiva— who possesses the forms of all that is knowable— is like a crystal;
because he pervades all internal and external entities, whether they exist within his own substratum or elsewhere on some contracted level, as they are reflected within him.

The intention of the Sūtra is that [the ālayavijñāna] is like the life-force, because its existence is established by the fact that it provides the manifestation and existence of those [seeds], and its continued presence would otherwise be impossible. [This refers to] the Lord, whose nature consists of all seeds.

Because of its identity with the nature of consciousness belonging to its own class, the bearer of all bodies exists as distinct from the body, like a reflection in a mirror. (1.63)
He for whom the visible world exists as a pervasive [manifestation] is the abode of the glory of liberation.
Having thus stated the true nature of knowledge and its yoga, how could it be otherwise? (1.64)
And he states the aphorism for that purpose, concerning him who is to enter the temple of his own heart:
"From the friction of the mind within the heart, there is the vision of the wild beast of the visible world. (1.15)
In the heart— which serves as the foundation and the locus for the continuums of all the sense-faculties and channels—

there occurs the dissolution of the perceived objects of no benefit through the focused attention of a mind that has become detached and ceased from external objects pertaining to this world and the next, by means of practice and so forth. Or else:

The "space of deep sleep" (*sauṣupta-vyoma*), which exists as the boundary between the pure and impure paths—the upper and lower—is called the Heart (*hṛdaya*). In that state, which is devoid of mind and consists of neither light nor darkness—where...

Due to the absence of the sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth, there occurs as a natural consequence the cessation of the two activities— studying the Vedas and establishing social conventions— which are characterized by the terms *brahman* and *kṣatriya* that depend upon that [ego-sense];
and there is the realization of one's own immediate intrinsic nature within the space of the Fourth (*turīya*).
There is also the cessation of ignorance, which is the root of the misfortunes of saṃsāra such as birth and death.

For one whose mind is unawakened, however, there is the experience of sleep therein. This is the intended summary of the verses of the *Kārikās* that explain the meaning of the aphorisms beginning with "in the substrate" (*ādhārabhūte*). [In the heart.]

When he is dissolved into that space with respect to his body,
then the killing of a Brahmin or a Kṣatriya remains attached to him as a consequence.

through the penetration of the divine mudrā, the omnipresent Lord is forever awakened. (1.70)

The unbroken, circle-shaped, and perfectly full [reality] resides within the hand;

"And one's own light (or one's own world) shall not diminish," so the All-pervasive Lord declared in three Sūtras. Through the abandonment of external egoity, one’s own state remains unbroken;

Since external [manifestation] occurs through the mere will of the entities residing within,
there exist five powers preceded by will, knowledge, and action. (1.89)
Īśānī, Āpūraṇī, Hārdī, Vāmā, and Mūrti—these are considered [the primary powers];
the others, known as Vijñānadehā and so forth, are recorded as their followers.
The construction of the body through the process [of these powers] is called their conjunction. || 1.90 ||
While that exists, for whichever part of the body it exists in, and in whatever manner it is situated— || 1.91 ||
Thus, its birth may likewise be distinct from that of animals, humans, and gods;
in this way, its agency everywhere remains entirely unimpaired and inexhaustible. (1.92)
Even in the light of truth, the perishability of conditioned phenomena has been demonstrated. (1-20)
Furthermore, this very [text] establishes its sovereignty through its manifestation. (1.93)
The Blessed One spoke this Sūtra, which describes his own desired play:

"The union of the elements, the separation of the elements, and the assembly of the universe— [that which is] this most clear consciousness-bliss, serving as the material cause for the pure path of the conscious Self..."

That very collection of powers of will, knowledge, and action is, on the lower path, the basis for the descent into the sequence of the *tattvas* by way of five groups of five; namely, through its own power, which has resorted to the state of *māyā* due to contraction during the manifestation of the state of nothingness (*ākiṃcanya*).

The conscious self (cidātman) has entered the stage of the principle of the individual soul (puṃstattva). The collection of powers (śaktinicaya), however, has become a sheath (kañcukībhūta) for the sake of enjoying the limited majesty appropriate to that state. Subsequently, for the sake of the continuous flow of the net of principles lower than that, by means of that [power] which subsists on the shadow of the three powers (triśakti)—

Through the manifestation of the transformation of the *guṇas*, there occurs the attainment of the state of the *puryaṣṭaka* (the eightfold city), which resides in the equilibrium of *prakṛti*. The principles of mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), and ego (*ahaṃkāra*) are the substrata for the triad beginning with will (*icchā*); this occurs precisely through the association with the five powers (*śakti*), due to the predominance of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
The manifestation of the cognitive faculties (*dhīndriya*) occurs, and due to the predominance of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), the organs of action (*karmendriya*) arise;

furthermore, their production occurs simultaneously with the external world in its gross form. In this way, the construction of the universe proceeds through various distinct modes, while a single [principle] remains inherent within those categories (*tattva*).

The nature of this conscious self (cidātman), which is a universal light and remains undivided despite appearing divided, is now described as it manifests its own desired play by assuming the stage of the eightfold subtle body (puryaṣṭaka) and thereby carrying out the drama of the universe. || 1-21 ||
The creation of the elements, beginning with space (ākāśa), occurs through the constituent parts such as the power of sound (śabdaśakti) and the rest. (1.94)
The "joining" (*saṃdhāna*) of those [elements] has been explained with the intention of describing their differentiation of forms.

Each individual element (*bhūta*) and its own existence (*svasattā*)—or rather, its own object (*svārtha*)—are said to be "oneness" (*aikya*), while their distinctness is called "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*); for that [separateness] is the most excellent portion of the agent (*kartṛ*).
[They] experience the touch known as joy and illumination through their functional activity, abiding in the ground [of consciousness]. (1.96)
The Sun and the Moon are to be known as the knowledge and action of the conscious, all-pervading Sacrificer (the Sacrificer who is the pervasive consciousness).
Likewise, the union with the totality of the universe in its suchness is desired through the four [powers].
Therefore, the manifestation of the all-pervasive Consciousness is the yoga of the creation of individual forms;
this entire universe here consists solely of the coming together of these eight.
How can the powers (śaktayaḥ) be the cause of the entire world, and how can the Self possess sovereignty over them? For this purpose, he has uttered the aphorism (sūtra). (1.99)
From the arising of pure knowledge (śuddhavidyā), there is the attainment of the state of a Lord of the Wheel (cakreśa). || 1-22 ||

Pure, free from substrate, the light that illuminates all manifestations. (Note: The sequence of words beginning with "jyotiḥ sarvabhāsa" and ending with "tatprathanam" was not present in manuscripts k and kh; it has been introduced here from manuscript ga. || 1-100 ||

Because He is the creator of infinite objects and possesses the nature of supreme sovereignty, His consciousness is described as *vidyā*, whose form consists of the awakening to "I am everything. (1.101)

Its arising is its manifestation; therefore, the accomplishment characterized by the Lord of the Wheel (*cakreśa*) occurs everywhere, with the sovereignty of Maheśvara expanding forth. (Note: The reading *siddhirbhavati cakrākhyā* is also found, as is a version lacking the word *māheśvaryeti*, resulting in a verse-line that is deficient by one foot.)
By directly realizing one’s own self as the Supreme Śiva— the dense mass of consciousness that is the unsurpassed and all-pervasive universe—

the yogi attains both supreme and non-supreme sovereignty. Through the attainment of His power, which unfolds as the supreme lordship of Maheśvara, [he realizes] those [powers] consisting of the eightfold sovereign powers, beginning with *aṇimā*.

The attainment of lordship over the Cakreśvarīs [is described]. Among these, through *aṇimā*, by means of a sudden reduction of limbs according to one's own will, the body is rendered subtle, such that there is the power to enter even into atoms. Through *laghimā*, one who possesses a most massive body becomes like a blade of grass or a tuft of cotton.

Movement through the masses of air; greatness, which is the state of having a large dimension; attainment, by which one touches the moon and other objects even while standing on the ground due to the lengthening of the fingertips through the accumulation of limbs; and irresistible will, by virtue of which there is no obstruction to one's desire, as if in water.
Even when sinking into or emerging from the earth, his form is not obstructed by the forms of material elements.

By virtue of his mastery (*vaśitā*), all beings become obedient to his commands. By virtue of his lordship (*īśitṛtā*), he rules over the origin, dissolution, and arrangement of the elements. By virtue of his ability to dwell wherever he desires (*yatrakāmāvasāyitā*)...
The persistence of the fundamental natures of beings occurs according to their respective volitions.
Alternatively, the "wheel" (cakra) is the wheel of powers such as Brāhmī and others, which is the form of the Goddess of Consciousness;
and by virtue of being its Lord, [the yogin possesses] the excellences of knowledge such as intuition (prātibha), which are well-known in the Yoga scriptures.
They are born; thus, the intention is that the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara), fully endowed with unimpaired sovereignty, shines forth.
This being so, how does the consciousness of the potency of mantra arise from this?
The Sūtra speaks of that which establishes the true nature of great heroism.

Through the continuous connection with the Great Lake (mahāhrada), there is the experience of the potency of mantra; for the very friction between the possessor of power and power, by virtue of its nature being unfathomable as the stream of the expansion of the emerging emission (visarga), it is metaphorically designated as the "Great Lake."

The quintessential core of all that exists within it is the jewel of the great mantra, which consists of the self-aware reflective awareness of "I," independent and free from conceptual construction; it is that extraordinary vitality (*vīrya*) which takes the form of the primordial and the final, the support of the universe, [to be realized] by those who are vessels for its enjoyment.

It is tasted only by the great yogins through the contemplation of the aforementioned form; the meaning is that it is the abode of rest, the state to be attained, whose essence consists of infinite signifieds and signifiers contained within the womb of the supreme speech (*parāvāk*). || 1-23 ||

The Supreme Self alone is pure consciousness, the embodiment of both the possessor of power and power itself; it is the very nature of emanation and the supreme ground for the arising of all beings. (1.104)
Devoid of spatial and temporal divisions, with an uninterrupted continuity, it is called the "Great Lake" because of its similarity to a vast lake. (1.105)
That is declared to be the uncreated power within oneself; and therein, it is characterized by the essential savor of the middle tone, which is the fire-stick for the bliss of vision. (1-106)
And by means of the expanding and emerging power known as *śakti*, stability is attained within the lunar portion; that is the entry of *udāna*. (1.107)
When there is a continuous connection with that reality, then one's own state, in which the form of the desired object of knowledge is internalized, becomes established therein. (1.108)
The unfolding [of consciousness], whose form is a sprout emerging from the state of perfect emptiness, consists of subtle speech; it is that in which the phonemes are not yet manifest. (1.109)
Through the application of the function of the half-measure of the letter *ka*, the emergence of the mantra occurs clearly;
that itself is the experience of vitality (*vīrya*), the mantra which bestows accomplishment upon the practitioner.
This first section, the *Śivasūtra-prakaraṇa*, which establishes that the essential nature of reality is the single light of universal consciousness, is completed. 1-111.
Beyond this, the essential nature of mantra is described,
endowed with the arising of knowledge (*vidyodaya*), in the section that follows. (1.112)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Determination of the Nature of the Universal Radiance of Consciousness," in the *Śivasūtravārtika* composed by the venerable teacher Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, son of the illustrious Bhaṭṭa Divākara. || 1 ||
Now begins the second chapter, titled "The Arising of Innate Knowledge."

Having established, according to the sequence already stated, the state of Śiva— endowed with all knowledge and action— within the self, one should consider what kind of mantra-power (*māntra-vīrya*) exists therein. (2.1)
Furthermore, it must be stated here that which is the mantra’s own form.
What is this mantra, whose potency the unborn Lord [assumes] for its sake? (2.2)
The mind is the mantra;
this aforementioned means is easily attained by those possessing an intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*) and the like,
but for those with a mild descent of power, they must repeatedly enter into the potency of the mantra.

Through the purification of conceptual thought— proceeding from a state of lack of clarity due to the influence of hearing, recollection, and so forth, until the attainment of the highest degree of clarity—
an alternative means consisting of the contemplation of mantras and the like [is employed], by which the experience of the supreme vibration [of consciousness] occurs.
When the manifestation of duality subsides, innate knowledge (*sahajavidyā*) arises; for the sake of attaining the state that is the goal,
consciousness itself first begins its desire to sport as the universe, descending from its own timeless, purely conscious plane into the lower worlds.

That which assumes an orientation toward an object of thought that has been manifested and contracted by first grasping a limited state is called "citta. Furthermore, when it desires to ascend to its own [original] state, it proceeds by the sequence of climbing a ladder and so forth.
Abandoning limitation, she whose nature is sovereignty becomes Śiva, who consists of the density of the light of consciousness.

Therefore, having withdrawn the object of knowledge, that mind— by virtue of its inward-turned state and its inherent freedom— is capable of grasping its own splendor, because its very essence is the act of such self-grasping.
[There is a metaphorical identification of the mind and the mantra. || 2-1 ||
Mind alone is to be known as Śiva, the subject free from limiting adjuncts (upādhi),
possessing qualities such as omniscience, and devoid of the limitations of space and time. (2.3)

Because it possesses the nature of the experience of one's own self, it is sung as "mantra. [The half-verse beginning with] "How then... does not exist in other manuscripts; it has been interpolated from manuscript *ga*. Regarding how that might be accomplished by yogins, the Supreme Lord said:
Effort is the means of accomplishment. || 2-2 ||

Upon the immersion of the mind into form, through the repeated withdrawal of external mental fluctuations and preceded by the dissolution of perceptions distinct from the knower and so forth, there arises the very state of a continuous flow consisting of the single-pointed concentration on the realization of identity with the internal form of the aforementioned mantra-sound.
The meaning is that it is the most effective means for attaining the goal; effort is thus defined as excellence. (2-4)
Through the application of the previously mentioned vigor, by means of further repeated observation, that very practitioner is proclaimed there as the most excellent. (2.5)
The nature of consciousness belonging to the Self is established by the reasoning that will be explained hereafter;
it has been described by Śiva himself in the *Trikasāra*, a work of six thousand verses. (2.6)
That which is the very nature of the power of consciousness (cicchakti) is celebrated as Mantra;
by the continuous contemplation of which the yogi becomes established on the ground of Śiva.
It is by virtue of this that yogis who contemplate yoga become knowers of the ultimate reality.

Having thus instructed [them] regarding the nature of the expressive words, the Blessed One [taught] whether the form of the expressed and the expressive is non-different or characterized by difference. (2.8)
For that purpose, he spoke the Sūtra which illuminates that very meaning:
"The existence of the body of knowledge is the secret of mantra. (2-3)
When [the mind] is purified, that sudden unfolding which occurs through immersion in pure consciousness alone— || 2-9 ||
That which is called the expansion of self-luminosity is defined as *vidyā*;
it is the existence of the body as mantra, and that is the supreme secret. (Thus, for the practitioner who desires to penetrate the potency of mantra, because of its being the locus of duality...)

The mantra, manifesting as the nature of the signifier (*vācaka*), is indeed non-different from its signified (*vācya*)—which consists of the vibration of the essence of the full self-reflection (*pūrṇāhaṃvimarśana*) comprising the non-duality of the entire universe—immediately following its own operation. This is according to the principle stated [in the *Trika*]: "Prior consciousness is transformed into the vital breath (*prāṇa*)."

The power consisting of supreme speech (*parāvāṅmayī śaktiḥ*), whose nature is the *bindu*, having assumed the state of the subtle vital breath (*sūkṣmaprāṇatā*) in the form of *nāda*— which is the expansion of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*)— and containing within it the supreme *nāda*, unfolds the state of *paśyantī*, in which the sequence of signifier and signified has not yet arisen, through the predominance of the light of consciousness (*citprakāśa*).
Thereafter, by means of the clarity or lack of clarity of the sequence of the intellect's substrate,

he unfolds the *madhyamā* speech, and even beyond that, the *vaikharī* speech— which is characterized by the instruments of articulation and possesses a manifest sequence— since this entire process of unfolding follows the nature of its primordial source.
The meaning is that the circle of mantras is indeed non-different from the supreme denotable reality (vācya), because its state of being manifest would otherwise be inexplicable. || 2-10 ||
This being the case regarding the secret reality in the form of mantra,
according to each individual's capacity, that very mantra-method [is employed] by embodied beings.
"The supreme arising" (paramodaya): this supreme arising of mantra is what embodied beings must seek. || 2-11 ||
How might the All-pervasive Lord (Vibhu) be present here? The Sūtra states it as follows:

"In the womb, there is the expansion of consciousness, which is a distinguished sleep of ignorance" (*Śivasūtravimarśinī*: "In the womb, the expansion of consciousness is a distinguished sleep of ignorance").
Such is the reading that exists. || 2-4 ||
By the power of turning away from within that which has light and bliss as its essence, intensely. || 2-12 ||

The state of the mind, consisting of consciousness, belonging to one who has withdrawn from sense objects (this half-verse beginning with "viṣayebhyaḥ" and ending with "vilopanam" was extracted from manuscript *ga*).
The supreme expansion is filled with the nectar of the moonlight of the moon of consciousness. || 2-13 ||
Pervading the world, he is one who rejoices, being flooded by the fullness of the nectar of the Śrāvaśakti;
because of the presence of that [nectar], ignorance is expanded through the elements beginning with earth. (2.14)
By means of the method of complete immersion through the nets of reality, it is like a dream or a boat;
this being so, knowledge itself has been correctly expounded. (2.15)
Therefore, this system (*mata*) is accompanied by the means (*sopāya*), as it consists of all mantras and mudrās.

In the *Mantrodaya*, through the destruction of the mind's ordinary nature, the three states produced by its qualities are dissolved; thus, there occurs an immersion into the exceedingly lofty supreme state (*atyunnataparapadāveśa*).

Established usage (*ruḍhi*) is the means. Thus, when vigor (*vīrya*) has been attained, the application of power is employed for the fulfillment of the objectives of other mantras that have been revitalized by it;
otherwise, there would be the joining of mantras to the Self and Śiva as they exist in a state of mutual hierarchy.
The sense is that, by producing dullness and fruitlessness, it would indeed fall into futility. || 2-4 ||
The potency of mantra, its essential nature, its reflective awareness, and likewise its arising. || 2-16 ||
Having thus explained [the previous matter], Śaṅkara spoke again for the sake of the power of the mudrās.

Upon the spontaneous arising of knowledge, there is the state of Śiva known as Khecarī; by means of this, the yogi moves within the space of supreme consciousness (paracidākāśa), and thus it is the Khecarī Mudrā, which is the direct state of Śiva itself.
Here, through the pacification of all disturbances pertaining to Māyā, the potency of both Mudrā and Mantra is realized.

The meaning is that there exists an equilibrium of states characterized solely by the emergence of one's own nature as consisting of consciousness; however, due to the difference in effects regarding the cognition of external objects, they are perceived as having distinct referents. || 2-5 ||
That very Vidyā which has been described is pure, characterized by its own light. || 2-17 ||
The arising of that [power] in its origination has been correctly explained previously. Natural power is innate, inherent in the self, and uncontrived. (2-18)
This being so, that very vigor of the mudrā unfolds therein;

for that Khecarī is the state of Śiva, having arisen in the void of Śiva. (*Note: The half-verse beginning with "tadevam" is not found in other manuscripts, but has been included here based on manuscript 'ga'.*)
It is fulfilled. || 2-19 ||
Because she moves within the expanse of the sky of consciousness (*svacidgaganābhoga*), she is called "Sky-farer" (*khecarī*);
her nature consists in the arising of the realization of identity with the form of the object of meditation. (2.20)
Therefore, the state of Śiva is characterized by immersion into one's own true nature. (2.5)
In this way, both physical and mental vigor would become of one form. || 2-21 ||

Because it possesses distinctions due to the difference in its functions, and because it brings about the comprehension of external objects, he therefore speaks [of these] for the purpose of the means of pervasion through the potency of mudrās and mantras: || 2-22 ||

The Guru is the means. [In this context, the Guru is the grace-bestowing power of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvarī anugrāhikā śaktiḥ) which, through the attainment of the power of mantra and so forth, leads one to the state that is the goal; by means of her, the devotee comes to rest in the unsurpassed state of the Unmanas, known as Paramaśiva. || 2-6 ||
In this context, regarding attainment (*prāpti*), the Guru is remembered as the supreme power (*śakti*) and means (*upāya*);
for that power of Śambhu is always bestowing grace (*anugraha*). (2.23)
A living being is protected from calamities and rendered free from desire for worldly existence;

with his body presided over by that [deity], he is led toward a true guru. (From the verse beginning with *vaktṛtvāt*... [He is led] because of the teacher’s capacity to speak the ultimate truths and because of the attainment of the state that is the goal.
This half-verse, not found in other manuscripts, has been collected and presented from manuscript Ga:
"The Guru is the one who shows the path of rest in the transmental (aunmanasa) abode. (2.25)
When the Guru is thus pleased, what will happen? That is now demonstrated:
the awakening of the Mātṛkā-cakra. (2-7)
The Mātṛkā, which is self-luminous, should be known as the supreme power of action (kriyāśakti) of the Lord.
The collection of its parts is celebrated as that wheel; [it belongs] to Paramaśiva, whose form is the Absolute (Anuttara), who, desiring to emanate the universe by his own will,
possesses [that wheel] which is non-different from him and consists of the first vibration characterized by the reflective awareness of his own nature.

The power of action (kriyāśakti) exists, known as Mātṛkā; having contemplated that very [power] in the form of the fourfold energy consisting of Ambā, Jyeṣṭhā, Vāmā, and Raudrī, [one perceives] that which is about to arise through the mutual intermingling of the expansion and repose of the digits (kalās) such as Dhruvā, Icchā, Unmeṣā, and so forth.
Having caused the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*), which consists of the seed-syllables (*bīja*), and the *bindu*— whose nature is the realization of non-difference from that—

to emerge, she manifested the *visarga*, whose form is the desire to emit, [projecting] the impure path (*aśuddhādhvan*) consisting of the emergence of the power (*śakti*) whose essence is the womb (*yoni*).

He elaborates: therein, upon the descent of the will-power (*icchā-śakti*)—which encompasses the entire wheel of powers—into the nature of vital breath (*prāṇa*), there arises the activity of the vital breath which contains words, sentences, and so forth, preceded by the manifestation of the unstruck sound (*anāhata-dhvani*). Therefore, the *mātṛkā* alone [is the source] of all this.
The meaning is that she is the expander of the universe consisting of the signified and the signifier, and the primary primordial cause of the mantras.
