The thorough comprehension of that is held to be perfect awakening. (2.27)
When that [consciousness] exists, there occurs a manifestation characterized by the relationship between the signified and the signifier;
because it arises from the power of action (kriyā-śakti), it is both distinct and non-distinct from the eternal source. (2.28)

From the Lord, whose nature is an eternally risen and never-setting light, there first arises the manifestation of the power of will (icchā-śakti) due to His orientation toward creative emission (visarga-unmukhya). (2.29)
From that, sensation and touch manifest;
from that again, the appearance of all objects; and from that, the unstruck sound (anāhata).
From that, the action, which consists of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and contains the meaning of words and sentences,
arises; from that, speech, which contains the fifty phonemes, [arises] for everyone.
Within the interior of the fifty phonemes, there arises the manifestation of the entire universe. (2.31)
Therefore, Mātṛkā alone is traditionally held to be the single root of the entire collection of entities, such as mantras; thus does the power of action (kriyāśakti) of Śiva manifest. (2.32)

When the awakening to the wheel of the Mothers (*mātṛkācakra*)— or rather, the wheel of the subjects (*pramātṛcakra*)— has thus arisen, then whatever that awakened Lord speaks, he attains the state of the sovereign of mantras. Thus...

Whatever speech there may be— whether mundane or even this [sacred] discourse— from one who possesses perfect awakening and is fully enlightened, that too should flow forth without restraint for the accomplishment of its own purpose, like a mantra. || 2-33 || 2-7 ||
When the splendor of mantra has been thus fully kindled, Śaṅkara spoke regarding the karmic body there, which brings about rebirth. (2.34)
The body is the oblation. || 2-8 ||

The intention is that when the perfection of the mantra-body is attained, there is the destruction of the *kārma-mala*, which is the cause for bondage to the body. When [the fire] characterized by identity with the mantra has blazed forth, the physical body and the bondage of karma simply dissolve away. (2.35)
Therefore, having become the sacrificial oblation (*havirbhūta*), because it is the support for the divine body,
this very [body] is the supreme body of the conscious and all-pervading sacrificer (*yajamāna*).
The all-pervading consciousness. || 2-36 ||
In the Great Being who is without bolts [of obstruction] and in whom the great fire is eternally ablaze, there is the constant offering of the body and all categories of existing things. (2.37) (2.8)
Thus, what does he say regarding the food for one who abides in the supreme body of gnosis (*jñānakāya*)? [He says:

"In the state of supreme reality (*parāvasthā*), while cultivating the unfolding of the majesty of his own self (*svātmavaibhavavijṛmbhaṇa*), which is nothing but gnosis (*jñānamātra*), he is utterly free from desire; [he is] within and without his own self—"
Because its essential nature is full within this universe consisting of vibration; yet, in worldly transaction,

sometimes existing upon the stage of the body, like an awakened actor, it assumes the role of a character and performs dramatic enactments by means of the objects and the senses, preceded by the wonder of its own self.
The meaning is that, having brought forth the entire collection of objects permeated by the supreme nectar-like essence, he offers it to his own Self;
however, through attachment to objects, he does not forget the manifestation of his true nature and remain in a lower state like a beast. || 2-9 ||
In these two chapters, the supreme knowledge has been correctly explained. (2.38)
That very [reality] should be known as being like food, which brings about complete satisfaction; for through repeated contemplation of it, there arises a state of perfect fullness. (2.39)
This being so, what would result from the destruction of ignorance?
For that purpose, and for the sake of its accomplishment, the Lord worshipped by the immortals proclaimed this section. (K:
[the Great Lord] spoke of the section). || 2-40 ||

Regarding the dissolution of knowledge (*vidyā-saṃhāra*), there is the vision of dreams arising from that. Thus, through the contemplation of the meaning of the process described, when the undifferentiated knowledge characterized by limited omniscience (*kiñcijjñatva*) is submerged, those things produced from it—

By its own sovereignty, [consciousness] manifests the world of existence, non-existence, and so forth— which consists of conceptual constructions appearing as objects devoid of intrinsic nature— as being without material cause or causal complex, like a dream, in the variety of mountains, cities, groves, and the like.

The meaning is that the yogi, observing that those who are submerged and emerged within the mirror of the extreme clarity of consciousness (*saṃvedana*) are non-different from the existence of consciousness (*citsattā*), dwells without restraint like Śiva, possessing powers such as eternal omniscience, in the state where innate knowledge (*sahajavidyā*) has arisen. || 2-10 ||
For knowledge, which is experienced during the process of dissolution, is described as being undifferentiated. (2-41)

When its own self-luminosity arises, there must be the withdrawal of that [power]; for when withdrawal occurs, the collection of objects arising from ignorance—which causes delusion—ceases to exist. (2.42)
The vision of that [dream] is known as its dream-form (*svapnarūpa*); thus it has been summarized and described by the Supreme Lord. (2.43)

Upon the arising of a mental modification, there is awakenedness, a state that remains unrestrained, the nature of which consists in the manifestation of its own light; it is the oneness with the object of meditation and eternal contentment. (2.44)
This second section, which elucidates the arising of innate wisdom (*sahajavidyā*), the *Śivasūtra-prakaraṇa*, is now completed here. (2.45)
Therefore, the characteristic of the vibration of manifestation (vibhūti-spanda) must be explained here.
Upon attaining the power of the yoga of knowledge, he is like another wish-fulfilling gem.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Arising of Innate Knowledge" (*sahajavidyodaya*), in the *Śivasūtravārtika* composed by Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara Ācārya, the son of the illustrious Kashmiri Bhaṭṭa Divākara. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter, titled "The Pulsation of Manifestations."
Through the recognition of one's own true nature, through the power of mantra, and from the spontaneous arising [of consciousness],
the supernatural powers (vibhūtayaḥ) proceed; these are now being proclaimed.

The understanding [of this] through a consideration of what precedes and follows— (from "yo bodho'sya" up to "samācaṣṭa tadarthakam," comprising one and three-quarter verses not found in other manuscript sources; these have been collected from manuscript *ga* and presented here).
It unfolds;
through that blossoming, one becomes oneself the uninterrupted supreme bliss.
That by which the natural and manifest power of unimpeded sovereignty expands as manifestation— [the scripture] declares that [part] to be for that purpose.
In that regard, for the sake of first examining the nature of the mind, he said:
"The self is the mind. (3-1)

The knowledge of others' minds (manaḥparyāya) has been explained: when the mind is directed outward, it is reflection and conceptualization; when directed inward, however, it consists of the contemplation of one's own self.

The mantra: because there is an absence of distraction when [the mind] is turned inward, one abandons the contracted state of the mind and assumes its own innate nature as the conscious self (cidātman). Therein, through intensity, during the stage of practice, one is free from dependence on the functions of the senses.
Possessing unimpeded cognitive action due to the mastery of that power, he is able— like Śiva— to create externally,

for the perception of all people, any object conceived according to his will, without depending on earth, water, fire, and so forth; for the volitions and other faculties of one who is not liberated are not visible to others.

[The meaning is as follows: For one who is disciplined, even mantras and the like—though not manifest externally—are capable of revealing any object whatsoever, however difficult it may be to accomplish, because they possess qualities unique to the Śaiva tradition. [This applies to] the mind (*citta*) in every teaching.
Because it is a faculty (indriya), that volition (saṃkalpa) would be the mantra; thus it is called so.
When the self itself is to be known as the mind, devoid of speech and other faculties,
then that is to be known as the mantra which conforms to one's intention.
There can be no fulfillment of one's intentions through the mere contemplation of that [object's] own nature. (3-1)
For what reason is there no accomplishment of the mind's resolve? To this he says:
Knowledge is bondage. 3-2.
Knowledge is the mind that is distracted— its impurities of *rajas* and *tamas* not having been removed due to attachment to sense objects through passion and the like.
When one fails to attain the power of one's own self through the conquest of the primordial, real nature,
there is an absence of the soil that covers the light; consequently, one is unable to create intentions common to ordinary people, and thus attachment to sense objects alone persists.
The meaning is that it is the root of the obstruction to creation according to one's desire.
Due to contact with objects, that very thing— characterized by the manifestation of passion and so forth—
is the bondage of the mind, consisting in the veiling of its own true nature.
Internally and externally— (this half-verse beginning with "internally and externally" is not found in other manuscript sources and is presented here based on the 'Ga' manuscript)—
[this occurs] through non-attachment to sense objects and proficiency in practice.
When there is nothing to be thought of, then that seer of it is indeed liberated. 3-2.
Thus, what is said to be the obscuration of the eternal seer?
Māyā is the non-discrimination of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Kalā. 3-3.
The group of principles (tattva) beginning with Kalā and ending with the Earth is said to belong to this [Śiva];
since the entire universe is pervaded by these, they are therefore called "principles" (tattva) therein.
*Kalā* is proclaimed as a mere slight capacity for agency;
such a capacity for knowledge is traditionally known as the *vidyā-tattva*.
"This alone is desired"—thus passion (*rāga*) exists as a bond and a fetter.

In this present state of being, time (*kāla*) is considered to be the act of reckoning (*ākalana*). [Immediately after "time is considered to be the act of reckoning," it continues: "In regard to small collections of objects, *vidyā* is the capacity for knowledge."
The verse beginning with "kālo'dhunāditābuddhipravṛttiḥ kalanātmikā," which is observed in manuscript *kha*, appears to be an interpolated addition.
The necessity regarding the fruit of karma, the nature of the self as being determined by destiny,
the state of knowing pleasure and pain equally, and the predominance within the inner reality.
Pleasure, pain, and delusion are the qualities; the intellect consists of the capacity for reflection (or remembrance);
egoism is the state of self-assertion; and the mind is the faculty that impels the senses.
The group of cognitive faculties is known as the faculty of cognition (jñatva) as distinguished by the senses;
this group of active faculties, however, is the faculty of agency (kartṛtva) as differentiated by those very same [senses].
The group of subtle elements (*tanmātra*) likewise consists in the manifestation of mere sound and the rest;
from that which has emerged as distinct sound and so forth arises the group consisting of the five gross elements (*pāñcabhautika*).

The non-discrimination regarding these is *māyā*; by means of *māyā* alone, through the network of principles beginning with *kalā*, she constructs the sheaths (*kañcuka*), the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), and the physical bodies.

The nature of the eternally arisen self-luminous Seer is veiled for those individual souls (*aṇu*) who have been made to grasp the conceit of being limited subjects; however, for those who have transcended the plane of *māyā* by taking recourse to the practice of discrimination, [that nature is revealed].

Because it rests upon Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), there is the manifestation of one's own self as unobscured. Thereafter, through the cessation of bondage, there arises the previously mentioned authority over Mantra and the rest. For [the state] is deluding;
however, discernment (viveka) here likewise rests upon Pure Knowledge and the other [principles].
Therefore, the knowers of reality declare the pure principles (*tattvas*) [to be as follows]:
the principle of Śiva is self-luminosity, while the powers of perception and action are called *śakti*.
Sadāśiva is the fitness for possessing all ignorance and activity (*kriyāvartayogyatā*).
The principle of Īśvara is the state of being impelled; through that [principle], there is the act of sending forth.
For:
Vidyā is proclaimed here as the purity that consists in being the knower of the Śiva-scriptures and so forth;
by means of these [qualities] thus established in the Self, there is the conceptualization of the categories of reality (tattvas).
There is no fault in stating that the categories of reality (tattvas) possess that very state [of consciousness];
for this reason, reflective awareness (vimarśa) is therefore the supreme [reality], because it is the form that permeates everything. (3-3)
Having thus described the expansion of the Self in the form of the *kalās* which consist of reality (*tattva*),
he speaks again of how its arising occurs through contraction.
Śrī is the withdrawal of the kalās. 3-4.
The inherent capacity of the principles (*tattva*) is proclaimed as their *kalās*;
the aggregate of those [capacities]— within the body, which consists of an aggregate of principles—
at its conclusion, through the contemplation of the dissolution of the parts of the principles back into their respective causes in reverse order (*prātilomyena*).

Through absorption (*samāpatti*) into one's own self, which consists of consciousness and is the substrate of all things, there arises the body of supreme awakening; or else, through the forceful withdrawal of all mental fluctuations (*haṭha*), by means of a state of leaping-over (*ullaṅghana-vṛtti*) preceded by the attainment of a one-pointed state that abandons conceptualization, [there arises] the self consisting of non-conceptual consciousness.

The attainment of the state of sovereignty [is achieved]. Thus, by the withdrawal of the expansion of *kalā*—which is conceived as the subject (*pramātṛ*) and which is the cause of the obscuration of one's true nature and the lack of sovereignty—the sprout of *siddhi* (accomplishment) blossoms and shines forth; this is the meaning. Therefore, his body is characterized by *sakalatva* (the state of being accompanied by *kalās*).
In that context, the withdrawal (saṃhāra) is proclaimed to be the entry of the powers (kalās), which constitute the substrate of the self, into their respective instruments of action.
In this way, up until the attainment of the body of awakening (*bodhadeha*), there is the supreme arising;
or else, by means of the practice of leaping over (*ullaṅghanavṛtti*), one takes recourse in the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*).
Therefore, that would indeed be the withdrawal of the kalās; by that [means], there is the arousal. || 3-4 ||
Even though the Self has such a nature, consisting of both the expansion and contraction of reality, [it remains as it is].

Having established the emergence of His own essential nature through the method of transcending the [limited] functions, Śiva spoke again: "How does the arising of the accomplishment of the elements occur?"
The withdrawal of the channels, mastery over the elements, isolation from the elements, and the distinctness of the elements. (3.5)

In the support of consciousness— whether internally or externally at the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve finger-breadths)— for one who desires supernatural powers (*siddhi*), through the withdrawal of the *prāṇa* and *apāna* breaths and the pacification of the channels such as the *iḍā*, [one should practice] in the foundational seats (*adhiṣṭhāna*) such as the *kanda*, as described in the Tantric procedures.

For one who maintains the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) on earth and the other elements— shaped as triangles, circles, and so forth, and marked with their respective seed-syllables— the elements come under control through practice during fixed periods of time;
by means of this, his coming, going, and moving about among things composed of the five elements no longer [occur].

It is obstructed. Likewise, even for one who acts in this manner, through non-attachment to that sovereignty, the attainment of abiding in one's own self—which is a mass of pure consciousness and bliss, untainted by the elements—also becomes accomplished without effort. Thus, by his will, the reality composed of the principles [manifests].

It is separated and it is joined; thus, with its sovereign power unimpeded, it has the autonomy to bring about various states and transformations—both altered and otherwise—of those things born from the physical body that is a manifestation of its own self. [While this body remains established...]
In that which consists of the five elements,
the self possesses sovereignty by virtue of its independence, just as the master of a house has ownership over his home.
In that state, the withdrawal of the channels (nāḍī-saṃhāra) is desired through their dissolution into the space of consciousness (cidākāśa),
since that is said to be the opening of all the channels everywhere.
The winds have the channels as their support, and the all-pervading consciousness is the support of those;
through the dissolution of its activity within [the central channel], there arises the supreme sixfold activity in the middle.
Solidity, fluidity, heat, mobility, and porosity—
these are the essential natures of the elements, or alternatively, they are distinguished according to their locations and specific characteristics.
By contemplating [the self], one who is awakened and a lord shall achieve mastery over the elements;
and through the very rejection of those [elements], his unconditioned liberation (kaivalya) is attained.
The manifest reality, endowed with the power of the thirty-six principles, acts individually through the touch of its own strength, by means of the evolution and involution of its own manifestations.
Furthermore, the omnipresent Lord transforms that which resides in the aggregate as well as that which resides in the self;
therefore, this power of sovereignty belongs to Him whose nature is everywhere undivided. (3.5)
Nevertheless, Śaṅkara has declared whether or not the establishment of this Self's true nature occurs while its delusion spreads in many branches:
"Establishment [occurs] despite the veil of delusion, through ultimate inquiry; [it concerns that which] resides on the lower plane."
The manifestation of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and the like, which serves as the locus for the perception of duality, falls entirely within the realm of *māyā*;

for that indeed obscures the true nature (*svarūpa*) of the yogin. Therefore, in order to perceive that [true nature], there must be the emergence of mental states such as intense joy, desire, and so forth during that state.

The meaning is that when their own true nature is concealed, by fixing the mind upon either their initial limit or their final limit, the supreme perfection characterized by omniscience and other qualities shall be attained.
In the arising of desire, anger, greed, joy, fear, terror, and intoxication,
as well as in every instance of intense exhilaration, it is delusion alone that prevails.
That very [state] should be known as an obscuration because it conceals one's own nature; for that reason,
it exists prior to the primordial awareness that serves as its cause.
There shall be the attainment of the self characterized by omniscience and agency. (3.6)
When delusion (*moha*) exists, there is no accomplishment; thus, what does he say regarding its conquest?

Through the conquest of delusion, by means of infinite expansion (*anantābhoga*), there is the conquest of innate gnosis (*sahajavidyā*). For one who is perfectly awakened, this arises from the conquest of delusion—which is characterized by being unconditioned and complete, and is called the pacification of the manifold divisions of branches—from which infinite expansion proceeds.
There occurs the arising of artificial *vidyā* (knowledge) known as the consciousness of the full self-reflexive awareness (*pūrṇāhaṃvimarśasaṃvit*). Alternatively,

by reason of conquering delusion (*moha*), one attains the perfection of innate light (*sahajāloka*) after occupying the plane of pure *vidyā*, which is presided over by the Lord Rudra known as Ananta Bhaṭṭāraka.

For in the state of Śuddhavidyā, sovereignty is enjoyed everywhere by the subject Rudra, who bears the name Ananta; thus, here, because of the elision of the suffix *lyap*, the case is that of the ablative (*apādāna*). || 3-7 ||
Delusion has been described as having many branches; its conquest is supreme awakening,
occurring through the constant power of one's own light, due to the uncontracted movement of consciousness.
Therefore, from that which is called infinite enjoyment (anantābhoga), the arising of self-luminosity is clearly manifest;
for from it, victory’s infinity unfolds with many branches.
That very [state] is called "enjoyment" (ābhoga) by virtue of its complete nature;
it is the innate (sahajā) knowledge whose essence is self-luminous, as previously described.
Its arising (*udbhava*) is its emergence (*prodgama*); by that, the self-illumination (*ātmāloka*) is supreme. (3-7)
Thus established in perfection, he should remain ever awakened and unwearied, concentrating everything upon that single goal; for this purpose, the Unborn One (Aja) has spoken.
He who makes the waking state his second hand. || 3-8 ||
Knowledge is said to be the waking state; having perceived its own object through that, one should take up everything from a single perspective, thereby remaining free from delusion.
The king of yogis, free from all duality, should remain perpetually awakened;
for by the gravity of his grasping during the waking state, his hand is indeed like his very self.

For this very reason, its second nature is proclaimed due to its manifoldness. According to the principle of the previously stated aphorism, "Knowledge is waking," waking here refers to the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). However, previously...

Having explained this by way of the relationship between the subject (*anuvādya*) and the predicate (*vidheya*), it is now explained by way of the predicate being the subject, because the aphorisms are "facing in all directions" (*viśvatomukha*).
Through the similarity to the act of grasping (*ādānakriyā*), the mind— which consists of the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*)— [perceives] form and light within the hand.

Having reflected that whatever universe is manifested by the agents of cognition is non-different from the supreme light— according to the logic that it is free from the conceptual constructions of difference and non-difference— the awakened one perceives everything, both external and internal, as consisting of his own self within a single consciousness.

The meaning is that, perceiving the entire universe as resting [in itself], becoming a vessel for the glory of liberation, and engaging in the conduct of one liberated while living, one should dwell in one's own self alone. || 3-8 ||
Thus, for one who is eternally awakened, the Goddess of Delusion, though long departed,
continues to dwell within the body at all times, even for one who is liberated while living.
Therefore, how does the Self, ever intoxicated by the essence of supreme bliss, act? For that purpose, the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva) explains the Sūtra.
The self is like a dancer. || 3-9 ||
One who is proficient through the cultivation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*),
and who is endowed with vocal expression, physical gestures, costume,
and inner disposition, is proclaimed as a true follower of the art, just like a skilled actor.
In the same way, the Self, flashing forth by its own nature, shines everywhere;
through immersion in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of this or that state of being, it possesses the playful manifestation of various activities.

He is considered a dancer because he takes up all states; thus, while sporting, reeling with the essence of supreme bliss, like a master actor who knows the aesthetic flavors (*rasas*), the emotions (*bhāvas*), their semblances (*ābhāsas*), and so forth, he assumes the role of the limited subject as his own dramatic character.

Manifesting the objects of imitation— such as rasa, bhāva, and so forth— through physical gestures and other modes of representation while remaining entirely mindful of his own self, the actor who imitates all states is,
by means of the determinants (vibhāva) and other factors, brought to the state of being tasted, even without the desire for the attainment of the desirable or the avoidance of the undesirable.

The meaning is that, enacting the drama of the world through the successive movements of the senses, he sports with a mind satisfied by the power of his unimpaired vision, manifesting his own self everywhere. || 3-9 ||
Therefore, for the sake of providing a proper support for this dancing Self, he spoke as follows.
The inner self is the stage. || 3-10 ||
This Self, possessing the fortune of external expansion,
is called the dancer;
that which is its internal contraction is proclaimed as the inner self.
That very stage is so called because it is the locus of the *puryaṣṭaka*;
it is the stage where one takes delight with the intention of displaying various extensive dramatic performances,
and it is the place for assuming those various diverse roles— the inner self in the form of the *puryaṣṭaka*.

Taking that very [Śakti] as its support, the conscious Self (cidātman), having established its abode within the bodily planes of humans, animals, and so forth, performs the fivefold cosmic functions— such as creation and the rest— through the activity of the instruments (karaṇa), and thus dances.
The all-pervading consciousness dances here, as it were, through the processes of manifestation, maintenance, and withdrawal;
this being so, the aggregate of the senses cannot be its obscuration.
To that end, the Sūtra, which bears half the body of his beloved, further says: "The senses are spectators. (3.11)
Since the supreme Self, which is consciousness alone, is perfectly awakened and autonomous,
it is through its power that the senses exert themselves in their respective functions.

These [senses] are like messengers for the all-pervasive Consciousness as it dances; indeed, they have no power to veil its true nature, for the independent Self of Consciousness alone is the illuminator of the instruments [of perception], since everything becomes manifest only through its illumination. It is that very [Self]...
If this entire universe did not subsist upon that which shines [the Self], it would become as if insentient, blind, and mute; therefore, the senses, vitalized by Him,
[experience] an abundance of supreme joy in manifesting the drama of the three worlds.
Having directly realized their own nature, in which the distinction between "I" and "this" has dissolved,
they bestow upon the yogi who perceives the inner self— like a sensitive spectator—
the wonder of the aesthetic relish (*rasa*) consisting of supreme nectar; by means of which, he does not [remain] like an ordinary person.

The wheel of the senses, whose nectar-like essence of the manifestation of non-duality is being covered by the *khecarī* and other [mudrās], is made to revolve within the path of the world consisting of suffering; therefore, the meaning is that the true nature of the conscious Self (*cidātman*), who thus dances, is not concealed. || 3-11 ||
This being so, it is for this reason that the Blessed One spoke the Sūtra, so that by the power of his intellect, the Supreme Person may indeed prevail as the most exalted of all.
The perfection of the *sattva* [element] results from the power of the intellect. (3-12)

The intellect (*buddhi*), while the sense organs continue to have their nature of constant outward flow toward objects such as sound, determines— by means of scriptural authority, reasoning, and so forth— that the objects such as sound which are reflected in its own modifications (*vṛtti*) are not distinct from its own conscious nature (*cinmaya-svabhāva*).

The meaning is that, through the exhaustion of other latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), the absence of impurity caused by the fluctuations of *rajas* and *tamas* brings about a yogin who perceives everywhere his own light as the supreme illumination, and who becomes the locus of the radiance of the essence of being (*sattva*) characterized by its throbbing vitality.
When the mental modification (vṛtti) becomes intent upon the nature of consciousness,
then the intellect (buddhi) becomes determinative with respect to that very [object].
Because it exists previously, that very power of consciousness (dhī-śakti) is called pure;
because the sattva has abandoned its latent tendencies (āśaya), it is called the foundation (bhitti) and the limit (avadhi).

Through the power of that [meditation], the accomplishment of the being (*sattva*)—or rather, the foundation or purification of the being—will occur; for this very reason, it has been so described. (3-12)
This being the case, the self would possess independence; therefore, he said: "The state of independence is established. (3.13)
His sovereignty is established by the method already explained;
for by him the entire universe, from Śiva down to the earth, is sustained, perceived, illumined,
and maintained under his own control— this is his state of independence, arising from innate knowledge and agency.

He is of a nature that brings everything under his control. Just as any object, when touched by a perfected alchemical elixir (*rāsāyanikī auṣadhī*), attains the state of gold, so too the universe, when permeated by his contemplation of the essential nature of Śiva, remains under his control; this is the meaning.
Just as it is in this body, so it is because of its possession of the activity of omniscience.
"It may exist everywhere, or it may not; regarding this, the Moon-Adorned One (Śiva) has declared:
'As it is there, so it is elsewhere.'"

Just as omniscience and other qualities manifest within a body presided over by the Self, so too do they manifest everywhere through the power of one’s own self-mastery; for this qualified practitioner,
who remains while contemplating his own supreme Śiva-nature within this body over which he has authority.

[The powers] such as omniscience and the capacity for action [arise]; thus, by the power of ascending into one's own self, omniscience and the other [powers] manifest without obstruction everywhere, even in bodies that are considered to belong to others. || 3-14 ||
Thus, for the independent agent who enters into the cities and other abodes of others, [there is no contradiction].

For this [self], when endowed with those qualities, there would be a state of remaining in an improper place (*akālapada*). (The two words *viśataḥ* and *taddharmopahitaḥ* do not appear in other manuscript copies of the root text;
they have been introduced based on manuscript G.)
How so? To that end, Kālāri spoke a sūtra according to its true meaning:

Because of the inherent nature of the *visarga*, its state [is established] by virtue of being situated outside [of it]. (The sūtra "visargasvābhāvyāt" does not appear in the *Vimarśinī* text; it has been collected and explained by the author of this very work. || 3-14 || 3-2 ||
In this state of consciousness, there arises from the nature of creation— which is the form of consciousness— through the process of activity,
that which has taken on the body of time, namely vibration itself.
And there would be no birth for that which is born of volition, because of the absence of such volition. (3.61)

Because external and outward objects lack any separate existence [beginning from "bahirbāhya" up to "yoganibhālanāt," this reading consisting of one and a half verses is not found in other manuscripts; G].
Having been extracted from a manuscript, it has been presented here.
[For those] who are to be enlightened and who tread the path of the contemplation of the oneness of light—
