Through the contemplation of yoga, there is no falling away from one's own abode; that very [power] born of desire at the improper time arises from taking recourse in the state beyond time. For the Supreme Lord, whose nature is the desire to emit, [projects] that which pertains to the objects of emission, submerged within himself, as his own support.

Even while manifesting that which is perceived as non-different from itself, it never undergoes forgetfulness of its own nature; for even on the plane of Māyā, the manifestation of the object of knowledge,
being in reality inseparable from the supreme light, remains situated within [the Self] and, through its sovereignty, appears externally.

It shines forth. Therefore, the meaning is that for one who has realized the true nature [of reality], the state of being conditioned by the subject (dharmin) and its attributes (dharma) can never again take hold.
Therefore, he stated the cause for arriving at an inappropriate time:
"the fixing of the seed" (bījāvadhāna). (3-15)
The seed of the entire universe is traditionally held to be the supreme conscious self alone;
its discernment is attentive awareness by means of an attentive mind.
The attainment of that state at that time results from the abandonment of the persistent grasping of delusion and the like; thus,

it is precisely the focused concentration of the mind upon the state of Śakti— the cause of the universe— through firm and uninterrupted practice, preceded by the total eradication of the limited sense of ego.
The sense is that this is the means for attaining one's own nature, which is unconditioned by time.
[Page 58] Entry into the interior of the conscious self is the source from which all states of being arise.

Furthermore, Śaṅkara has stated here how this occurs through the practice of yoga: seated comfortably on his seat, he sinks into the lake [of consciousness] like those possessed of realized knowledge. [For the wise...]
For yogins who perform intensive cultivation with firmness through a mode of practice attainable by effort suited to yoga— which consists of entering within the conscious self—
even when the state of *kumbhaka* (retention) exists, which cuts off both flows [of prāṇa and apāna], there occurs the friction of the sun and the moon (*ravīndusaṃghaṭṭa*).
By means of the exhaling flow (*recaka-vāha*) characterized by the upward projection of the pure fire that is synonymous with *udāna*,
one sequentially transcends the lower and lower supports and so forth, until rest is produced in the station of the *dvādaśānta*; for this very reason, it belongs to *udāna*.

It possesses "fierceness" (*caṇḍatva*) because it burns away the fuel of duality, and "purifying power" (*pavamānatva*) because it is the cause of supreme purity; by relying upon that very [power], one effortlessly plunges into the ocean of the nectar of the consciousness of Śiva residing at the *dvādaśānta*, where the waves of the world's manifold variety surge forth.

For those who are intent upon the constant relishing of the flavor of uninterrupted enjoyment, there occurs the attainment of the unsurpassed state of Śakti, which is untouched by time; through the practice of the aforementioned means, that state—devoid of internal or external mental constructs and consisting of indivisible sovereignty—is brought about. || 3-16 ||
The purifying, pure, and fierce middle breath is the seat for yogis who possess prior knowledge, by means of the movement of the true fish.

And it was previously stated that one situated therein immerses oneself happily in that lake; its nature as a "lake" (hrada) is mentioned here because it is the source from which all states of being arise.
For this very reason, the seed-nature of that which is of the nature of consciousness has been defined;
here, attentiveness and penetration are cited as the two means.
Thus, for the sake of conquering death and desire, and for the attainment of the immortal state.
Thus, the repose within the aspect of the agent is that very indivisible sovereignty.
Therefore, it would follow that he is the agent; thus says the "stigma of the low-born" (Vṛṣalāñchana): "He brings about his own creation by means of his own mother. (3-17)
The innate power of the Supreme Lord is characterized by knowledge and agency;
its vigor and strength are the cause of the arising of phenomenal existence.
And therefore, she is the supreme power (śakti) of that possessor of power (śaktimat), the Mother of the World;
by means of her as his own mother, the All-pervading Lord creates his manifestation according to his own will.

Thus, by the power of his own sovereignty, he swiftly and sufficiently accomplishes that reality— which consists of the manifestation of the object and the subject as desired— through the great cultivation of the two previously mentioned means, namely, focused attention (*avadhāna*) and entry (*praveśa*).

By means of his own power (*svaśakti*), whose true nature consists of agency and so forth, and which has the habit of manifesting the appearance of the unprecedented (*apūrvollekha*), he who rests in that state (*tatpadaviśrānta*) is able to create; indeed, this very act of creation indicates his resting in the abode of absolute freedom (*svātantryadhāma*). || 3-17 ||
And thus, its nature at that time is perceived by the intellect as being shrouded by impurity.
He stated therein that through its destruction, rebirth no longer occurs;
for with the destruction of ignorance comes the destruction of birth. (3-18)
That which is to be experienced (or understood) as possessing a substrate is exclusively concerned with the objects of the categories.
That knowledge is considered impure; furthermore, it is the cause of rebirth.
There may be the destruction of that [bondage], which consists in the contemplation of the arising of innate knowledge;
through that, when it exists, there occurs the supreme manifestation of the self's sovereignty.
Therefore, by relying on one's own power, rebirth shall not occur;

this is *jīvanmukti*, a perfection that bestows the state beyond time. [Cognitive activity (*vṛttijñāna*), which is the means for attaining the fruit of the object of knowledge, is impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*) because it is inscribed with the forms of objective entities.]

Thus it is said that she alone is the binder; yet, by means of the contemplation of pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) which is its opposite, when one attains innate consciousness (*sahajasamvit*) and thereby recovers one's own potency,
[the aggregate consisting of the body, senses, and so forth], which was accompanied by the two impurities of *āṇava* and *māyīya*, [is liberated].
The meaning is that the bond of karma is utterly destroyed. || 3-18 ||
This [state] which is characterized by the experience of objects and stained by the adjuncts of external things is ignorance;
as for what the cause of its impulsion is, the Unborn (Aja) has stated here: [it is the power of knowledge].
Within the groups beginning with the gutturals (kavarga) and so forth are the Mothers of the bound souls (paśu), beginning with Māheśvarī.
That form of the mass of sounds (śabdarāśi), which consists of all things and is composed of parts (kalā),
was previously taught as belonging to the bound soul (paśu) due to its permeation by sound.
That which correctly produces cognition is proclaimed to be of two kinds,
distinguished by seed (*bīja*) and womb (*yoni*); therein, Śiva himself is the seed.
Power (śakti), known as Māyā, is the womb consisting of the eight groups of letters from Ka to Kṣa;
therein lies the group of eight beginning with Māheśī, which bestows both supreme and worldly fruits.
Presiding over the perception of external objects by means of the senses,
it possesses terrible characteristics and generates attachment to the fruits of mixed karma.
For those whose minds are attached to sense objects, that [practice] leads further and further down into sin;
it may be most terrible or even more terrible, yet when free from cruelty (aghora), it bestows auspiciousness (śiva).

Thus, this group of eight measures (*mātrāṣṭaka*) consists of three divisions within each category. In the preceding category, the state of Bhairava resides as the imperishable Supreme Power of Speech (*parā vākśakti*).

Having manifested the triad beginning with Will (*icchā*) whose nature is non-different from Śiva, she unfolds the *Mātṛkā* consisting of the groups (*varga*) and their members; thus, within the state of conceptual cognition among the limited subjects (*paśu-pramātṛ*), she [manifests] the internal reflection upon gross and subtle sounds.
Acting through the presiding deities of the [five] groups, such as Māheśvarī and the others, she extends attachment,
aversion, desire, greed, and so forth, thereby effecting their very identification with the body and other such things; thus,
while the mental modification (vṛtti) proceeds by means of the instruments (karaṇa),...
The Mothers, known as Ghorā and others, beginning with Māheśvarī, cast the bound souls (paśus)—
who are turned away from their own Self— downward due to their attachment to sense objects; however,
they present to the Lords (patis) the essence of the expansion of their own Self, preceded by various forms of aesthetic wonder (camatkaraṇa).
The meaning is that they do not produce the manifestation of difference at all. || 3-19 ||
Thus, in this way, the aggregate of sounds (śabdarāśi), which arises from the eight groups (aṣṭavarga), possesses three natures.
The divisions of beginning, middle, and end exist in excrement as well as in the collection of phonemes;
he has taught that matter in such a way that, through non-differentiation therein, the state of Śiva may be realized.
The fourth [element] should be poured into the three like oil. 3-20.
Among the aforementioned divisions of the Mothers, which consist of the three castes,
he who alone remains here as the fourth is the supreme Śiva.
That [reality] should be contemplated and cultivated in the three [states],
like oil in water;
because its form is interwoven throughout them, there will be unfailing accomplishment, as determined by the previously mentioned sūtras.

One should perform a sprinkling with the essence of consciousness (cidrasa), which is perceived as the underlying substratum at the initial and final limits of the conceptual constructions consisting of gross and subtle phonemes, and which is presided over by the Mothers of the bound souls (paśu) known as Ghorā, Aghorā, and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: by means of the solidification of the essence of consciousness (*cidrasa*), its persistence is maintained; then, having dissolved the manifestation of duality, one should contemplate [the world] as consisting of the essence of consciousness, spreading further and further like oil to pervade its substratum, so that their own activity—which is of the nature of bondage—may be eliminated.
Regarding the means for entering into the phonemes (*varṇa*) therein,
he said:
"One who is immersed in one's own mind should enter [into them]."
Because the Lord of Consciousness (*cinnātha*), desiring to move toward extroversion,

possesses the power of vision and action that is actively expanding, there exists this state of functioning colored by objects; by withdrawing from that state, the yogi, through non-conceptual awareness (*avikalpasaṃvitti*), [perceives] according to the analogy of charcoal and fire.

One should effect the entry into the phonemes (varṇa). Through the successful application of the Bhairava-mudrā during this entry into the phonemes, even the vitalization of the mantra and other elements will be accomplished. || 3-21 ||

This state of assuming the form of external objects belonging to the all-pervasive Lord as He engages in manifestation is sufficient for the arising of the prior state through the yoga of its withdrawal.
When all activity has ceased, one should become immersed in one's own self;
thus, by the power of the closing of the eyes, having become Śiva through one's own mind.
One should enter the interval between those whose appearance is like glowing embers as if it were fresh fire;
furthermore, the supreme enlivening of the mantras occurs precisely through the activity of Bhairava.
This procedure applies not only to [the rites] in the cities of others and so forth;
and this being so, the nature of the mantras as Śiva and Bhairava is clearly evident.
Otherwise, why would the mantra, whose essence is phonemes, be the Lord? It vibrates [with power] precisely in this way. (3.21)
Thus, since the phoneme alone remains established through the exclusion of what precedes and follows it, what occurs? To explain that, the Lord [the author] states the Sūtra.
In the middle, there is the production (or expansion) of the lower [element]. (3-22)
When a phoneme is being uttered, it possesses three parts characterized as beginning, middle, and end; therein, the state of Śiva resides at both the beginning and the end.
Established by its very nature as both the desire to manifest and the state called rest,
there occurs in the case of the bound soul (*paśu*) a birth and a fall within the mere phoneme in the middle.
This very power of the Lord, whose nature is radiant, is taught as follows: in the desire to utter and in the cessation thereof—

characterized by the initial and final limits— the phonemes, which possess gross and subtle arrangements and fall within the domain of speech such as the *madhyamā* and others, [are dissolved] into the *paśyantī* and so forth.
Because they reside within undivided states, the nature of Śiva is achieved without effort.

However, in the case of the "middle category" (madhyakoṭi), due to the manifestation of various diverse forms and arrangements, there is a falling away from non-conceptual consciousness; this is the meaning. || 3-22 ||
This being so, in these three natures, how can there be complete equality?
Demonstrating this further, the beloved of Pārvatī spoke again:
In the conduct regarding the vital breaths, there is the vision of equality. || 3-23 ||
That supreme inherent capacity, whose form consists of all-knowing gnosis and action,
is the vital breath (prāṇa) known as the Supreme Sound (paranāda), capable of sustaining the life-force of all.
The practice of that [state] is an immersion (*āveśa*) vibrating within the atoms of phonemes and sounds;
through that, non-duality and direct experience are called "equal vision" (*samadarśana*).

Thus, having overcome that power, all things—such as phonemes and mantras—become endowed with the power of omniscience; what wonder is there in this? [This occurs through absorption into the independent Light known as the Supreme Sound (paranāda), which is the life-force of all manifestations.]

The meaning is that the attainment of supreme vitality (*paravīrya*) results from ascending the stream of practice in experiencing the non-duality of words, mantras, and so forth, which have extended down to the level of articulated speech (*vaikharī*).
Having thus defined the vitalization of the phonemes (*varṇānuprāṇana*), Śambhu spoke incidentally as follows:
Just as there is vitalization of the body of an entity and so forth, so it is here.
The re-emergence of that which was lost occurs through the non-connection with the conviction regarding the measures.
Having brought forth the portions (kalās) of the group of principles beginning with Māyā and ending with the Earth—
those portions of the principles from Māyā down to the Earth which serve as the material cause of the elemental body—
as consisting of the essence of consciousness through the continuous contemplation of their non-difference from one's own self;

The meaning is that even the splendor of phenomenal existence (*bhāvaśrī*), which has sound and other objects as its locus, arises as consisting of the essence of the dense mass of consciousness-bliss (*cidānandaghana*); by means of this, having attained the potency (*vīrya*) of entering the stage of universal agency and so forth, one presides over supreme sovereignty (*paramaiśvarya*) characterized by omniscience, omnipotence, and the like, everywhere.
Those which are the measures (*mātrā*) and those which are the manifestations (*vyakti*), each within its own sphere of perception for every respective principle (*tattva*).
Within those [powers], there is knowledge based on one's own direct realization; by that, each individual attains fulfillment.
This is the connection [of the teaching]; it belongs to its author and rests upon that [specific] ground.
When that exists, there is again the arising of a destroyed entity and so forth;
thus, by the power of the entry of the agent into the ground (or by the power of the agent’s excellent command), wherever it may be.

One should effect the unification of the measures and the cognitive conditions; thereby, there arises the state of being the agent, characterized by a firm establishment through the penetration of the power of omniscience and omnipotence. (3-24)
As to what such a person who is thus constantly disciplined becomes, he says: "He becomes equal to Śiva. (3.25)
Śiva exists at the head of the entire family of causes,
because he is eternally of the nature of unconditioned light by virtue of his being the very essence of consciousness.
Being ever-united with that [Reality], even while performing various activities, he is equal to it;
by the power of the previously mentioned knowledge, he becomes a practitioner liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). Thus...

For one who is eternally disciplined, because they have attained that state through the excellence of constant cultivation of the nature of Śiva, their Śiva-nature is compared [to actual liberation] by means of tasting the bliss of *jīvanmukti*, even while the subtle body (*dehakalā*) still exists. However, upon the transcendence of the experiences brought forth by *prārabdha* karma, there is indeed identity (*tādātmya*) with Śiva in the state of *videhamukti*.
The sense is that it is attained.
And for one who practices in this manner, what kind of constant application (*nityayuktatā*) does he possess?
For that purpose, the Blessed One spoke this sūtra which defines the vows.
Vow is the maintenance of the body. 3-26.
The body itself is a skeleton, a skull resting upon the bones;
the spinal column is the staff here, while the hands, feet, and neck are situated [like vessels] upon that staff.
Fragments of bone are the five mudrās; ash is known as the supreme radiance.
The three qualities (guṇas) are the sacred thread, and the great path is the banner.
The senses are its ornaments, and its ample diversion is among the sense-objects;
it is always attached to the cremation ground of the heart, throbbing with body, speech, and mind.
Whatever movement or vibration there is, that is always the festival of the Lord of Heroes.

This should be known as the Great Vow (mahāvrata) for one established in their own unobstructed state. By practicing according to the previously described method, the well-known Pāśupata Great Vow will be perfected—
[a vow] in which there are ornaments consisting of a skeleton, a skull, a staff, the five mudrās, ashes, a sacred thread, and a banner.
The collection of requisites for dwelling, wandering, and so forth, consisting of unmanifest substances, would be employed;

yet, by assuming manifest signs, he becomes a hypocrite (dharmadhvajī) and is smeared with the soot of impurity. Thus, regarding this observer of vows, he describes what his recitation (japa) is like: [text follows].
Discourse and recitation. || 3-27 ||
Whatever the awakened one, established in the state of the Knower, speaks—that shall be the recitation for the observer of the vow; through that recitation, he becomes the Supreme Person.
Recitation (*japa*) is said to consist of reliance on vigor, utterance, and movement;
thus it should be understood as fourfold: that pertaining to Śakti and that pertaining to the *haṃsa* (or *pudgala*).
[Even though he is partless,] here [he is] empowered by Śakti; this which is one's own [creative] activity (*svā haṃ-kriyā*) of consciousness—(the phrase *paudgala* is not present in the Ka.
and Kha. manuscripts immediately following this; the portion from *śākto'tra yeyaṃ svā...* to *kriyā citeḥ* is thus lost in the middle, with syllables missing at the beginning).
The reading of the verse text has been completed from manuscript *ga*.
The partless (*niṣkala*) *haṃsa*, situated within the limbs of the *praṇava*, consists of the essence of sound (*nāda*) and its subtle parts (*kalā*).
Known as the *jīva* and having the form of wind (*marud-rūpa*), it flows with its own activity for twenty thousand, one thousand, and six hundred [breaths] in an uninterrupted succession. Thus...

For this Vīreśa, who possesses the great vow and has ascended to the state of the contemplation of the supreme *ahaṃbhāva*, there exists— sustained by supreme vitality— the fourfold mantras consisting of the *niṣkala-haṃsa*, *paudgala*, and *śākta* forms.

The recitation (*japa*), which consists in the continuous turning toward the essential meaning of the awareness of one's own self as the deity, should proceed incessantly and must never be interrupted. (3-27)
Regarding what kind of gift such a perfected one— one who possesses this knowledge and is devoted to the vow of recitation— should give here in this world, Śaṅkara spoke on that matter:
Giving is self-knowledge. 3-28.
The conceptualization of the nature of the self is knowledge; that is supreme and most excellent.
It is the correct illumination of what has been said and what is yet to be said.
For those awakened by the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), that which is given here is the supreme gift;
from that gift, there occurs the complete destruction of the bonds (*pāśa*) of the bound soul (*paśu*).
The word *dīkṣā* used here is defined by the characteristics of giving (*dāna*) and destroying (*kṣapaṇa*).

For those who possess an intense descent of power (*tīvra-śaktipāta*) and who observe the prescribed vows of recitation (*japa*), [this occurs] according to the method that has been stated and will be stated.

It has been described that the very knowledge of the Self alone is to be revealed among bound souls (paśus); that itself is the true gift, because it is through this— characterized by the imparting of one's own essential nature and the destruction of the bonds such as the *āṇava* and others— that there arises eligibility for initiation (*dīkṣā*) among those to be graced.
"Thus it proceeds. || 3-28 ||
Thus, the all-pervading Lord performs creation, maintenance, destruction, protection, and grace.
Since the Self alone is of the nature of Śiva, the Holder of the Moon’s Crescent spoke this aphorism— both individually and collectively— to define its true essence.
That which is situated in the womb and is the cause of knowledge. || 3-29 ||
And as the source of the universe, the Supreme Lord alone abides,
whose nature consists of knowledge and action, because he renders that which is to be abandoned utterly insignificant.
Therefore, the yogi established in the state of the universal form, preceded by knowledge,
is declared to be the preeminent cause for both enjoyment and liberation.
The king of yogis who, through the correct non-attachment to the three realms,
has attained stability while remaining in the world— he is the supreme cause for the knowledge of that [reality].
In this context, those who are the bound souls (paśus), among them the group of Mothers is known as the Lord (pati).
The Self (ātman) abiding therein vibrates; therefore, He is the Lord of the Wheel (cakreśvara), the Supreme Śiva, the cause of the universe.

Thus, he whose nature is knowledge and action is the agent who effects the rendering of the discardable (the *heya*) as worthless; for by his grace alone, one established in the abode of the manifestation of the universe becomes a fit vessel for enjoyment and liberation through the presence of perfect subjectivity (*pūrṇajñātṛtva*) and other qualities. Or rather, [one becomes so] by attaining a firm footing through ascending to the level of the agent.

The Lord of Yogins is capable of awakening those to be instructed through the power of his own knowledge. Alternatively, within the groups of Mātṛkās such as Māheśvarī who preside over the limited subjects (paśus), it is the Self alone that flashes forth as the Lord of that wheel; [the scripture] refers to Him alone as its own rays.
The functions of consciousness presided over by the *mātṛkās* always worship [the Lord] by extracting the essential portion of the objects;
therefore, these *mātṛkās*, being dependent on Him and unable to obtain their own existence apart from Him, depend upon Him for their own manifestation— thus it is said.
The meaning is that it consists solely of the unfolding of power (śāktollāsa).
Thus, these functions of the Conscious Bhairava are known as rays;
they remain eternally present, worshipping Him through the enjoyments of objects such as sound and the rest.
In this regard, the cause is this knowledge of the group of Mothers; here, the all-pervading Lord is one's own consciousness.
Thus, that [text] states the universal form of this [reality], which consists of power: "by way of its being the universal form."
The universe is the accumulation of his own powers. (3-30)
In this way, the powers of this possessor of power—such as consciousness and the rest—are his own [powers] (variant k: of his own conscious self; variant kh: from his own conscious self).
The accumulations that are known as the throbbings of their ever-new manifestations—
These very [powers] are the universe to be known, since the All-pervasive Lord, whose nature is power,

manifests as the world-form while always shining forth by means of Himself; for just as the universe of Śiva consists of His own unsurpassed power, so it is for this yogin, owing to his equality with Śiva.

The power of self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*) has blossomed as the manifestation of the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), which consists of the vibration of a manifold and ever-new unfolding. All that is to be known— such as various blue objects, pleasures, and so forth—
whether manifesting externally or internally, rests upon repose within the Light (*prakāśa*).
Establishing itself, it would otherwise manifest the impossibility of its own realization;

thus, self-awareness itself vibrates everywhere by itself at will through the manifold variety of the universe in such and such ways. Due to the non-difference between power and the possessor of power, Śiva himself is thus.
The sense is that it shines forth. || 3-30 ||
Just as the Self is the creator of emanation, so too is it the sustainer and the dissolver;
demonstrating this, the Destroyer of Tripura spoke the following aphorism:
Stability and dissolution. || 3-31 ||
By means of those very accumulations of powers, whose nature is the manifestation of functional states,
the conscious Self alone brings about both maintenance and dissolution by its own will. (Thus, by its own power of will...)
The conscious self (cidātmā) effects the maintenance and dissolution of the universe manifested through the power of action (kriyā-śakti). In that process,
with respect to the subjects beginning from Anāśrita and the presiding deities of their respective levels up to the level of Śakti-tattva,
[the cycle continues] for a duration measured by a lifespan of various parārdhas, as long as there is an outward orientation.

The state called the manifestation of the universe situated below oneself occurs through the power of the non-fluctuation (*nimeṣa*) of the higher plane corresponding to each [level], whereby even one's own self undergoes dissolution; what need is there to mention the dissolution of the universe situated below that? Thus, dissolution consists in resting within the conscious subject (*cit-pramātṛ*). In this way, these two—[manifestation and dissolution]—are both...

The two things appearing [as subject and object] are nothing but the accumulation of one's own power (*svaśaktipracaya*). For the reason that the various classes of objects of knowledge, whether being closed or opened [to consciousness], cannot otherwise be manifested, they consist essentially of the power of consciousness (*saṃvicchaktyātmaka*); this is the meaning. || 3-31 ||
In this way, even during the times of creation, maintenance, and dissolution, the Self remains in its own state;
regarding how that occurs, Hara, the ocean of scriptures, has declared the following aphorism:
Even when that [cognition] arises, there is no negation [of the self], because of the existence of the cognizer. (3.32)
Even while these states of creation and so forth proceed, the all-pervasive Consciousness never abandons its own abiding state, because it is eternally the nature of the perceiver.
Non-abandonment here is non-annihilation; it is a qualification of the cognizer.
Thus, there is the annihilation of states, but never of the one who abides.
It would be described as having the nature of being pervasively continuous everywhere;
for even during the emergence of creation and so forth, there remains the persistence of the nature of consciousness.

It is never indeed cast aside from the state of the cognizer, which consists of the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) that brings about the wonder of the Fourth (*turya*). The word "that" (*tat*) is an elliptical expression for the fivefold activity (*pañcakṛtya*). The conscious Self (*cidātmā*), performing the fivefold activity, manifests the sovereignty of its own Self, which consists in the shining forth of each respective activity.

One should realize that one's own nature is eternally arisen as the witness of those entities whose very essence is perishing, by way of being the source of wonder at their prior and posterior limits.
Thus, for the imperishable abiding subject, there are only various states that repeatedly perish and arise.

They undergo transformation, but there is no destruction of that [substratum]. For if that were the case, its dissolution and so forth would be perceived as impossible, since they would lack a witness. This is the meaning. || 3-32 ||
Thus, regarding the investigation of pleasure and pain herein, he says:

The external mental application regarding pleasure and pain [is directed toward] the state of pleasure and pain in external objects. (k: [regarding] the state of pleasure and pain externally) || 3-33 ||

The experience of bliss arises through the attainment of desired objects and the like, such as the tasting of extraordinary sensory domains; thus, for one established in the state of the perceiver, there occurs a mental modification (*vṛtti*) of bliss born from the acquisition of contact with the most beloved worldly objects.
Conversely, the mental modification of non-bliss, which is suffering, arises from the failure to attain those objects and from the occurrence of their opposite.

Furthermore, that [limitation] is manifold, consisting of many divisions such as internal and so forth. Thus, although both of these have manifested, because of the firmness of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), they do not obscure one's true nature, since they are experienced as being devoid of "I-ness" and "mine-ness," like blue and other objects; they do not, however, affect this [subject] in the same way as they do for the limited subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*).
The meaning is that there occurs the touch of "I-ness" therein.
[Page 75] In the inner self (pratyagātman), [there is the experience] of external and internal happiness (or: directed toward the external and internal). (k: bāhyāntarmukhasya; kh:)
For one whose [mind] is turned inward, the external [objects] are considered to be "thought" (manana).
Suffering is threefold and fivefold, and furthermore, it is infinite through its various divisions;
that which consists of the triad beginning with the internal is indeed the three types of affliction.
Tamas, moha, mahāmoha, and tāmisra as the fourth;
and andhatāmisra is another—thus the eightfold nature is established here.
The conceit of self is *tamas*; the notion that the body is the self is considered *moha*.
*Mahāmoha*, however, is the identification of external things such as sons and so forth with the nature of the self.
Tāmisra is the lack of forbearance toward one who causes affliction to one's family and so forth;
the fifth is Andhatāmisra, which is the very terror of death.
For this very reason, through differentiation, consciousness again attains infinity;
because of the firmness of the entry of the agent into the earth [of the body], it assumes the form of identity with it.
Whatever intense mental agitation arises from any cause whatsoever, known as the states of pleasure, pain, and so forth, that shall become non-obstructive [to the Self]. (3-33)
Therefore, when that external mentalization does not enter within,
then what is the nature of the Self, which is liberated from that?
And so it has been said: "It might be thus."
But one who is liberated from that is a Kevalin. || 3-34 ||
And by means of those two, pleasure and pain,
as well as by the state of delusion, the Lord [is perceived].

Liberated, absolute, and established in its own nature through a state of activity that permeates all, when the internal mentalization of pleasure and so forth no longer enters, then, being untouched by pleasure and the delusion produced thereby,
with the glory of its own self undiminished, it is the supreme means of knowledge consisting of pure consciousness alone.
The meaning is that by resting in these three forms, the yogi experiences the fruit of yoga. || 3-34 ||
The state of delusion is either the concealer or not;
he has declared that the self consists of karma when it is bound by delusion. (3.35)
Delusion (*moha*), folly, lack of exertion, ignorance (*avidyā*), dullness, and obscuration— when,
by means of delusion as a synonym for ignorance, the conceit of selfhood (*ātmābhimānitā*) expands toward the body and other such things...

When one becomes pervaded by continuity, then, performing various mixed actions— both auspicious and inauspicious— assisted by the members of the body, while concealing one's own self which is of the singular nature of the full expanse of consciousness (*cidvyoma*), [one remains] through attachment to the fruits of diverse and manifold karmas.
The meaning is that one who is full of longing transmigrates through various wombs such as those of humans and others.
Furthermore, lack of discernment (*aviveka*) is expressed by these synonyms, such as *mūrchā* (fainting) and so forth.
The sense of "I" regarding the body and so forth expands only when [the self] is contracted;
yet the self is pervaded by it without interruption.
And he is declared to be the "action-self" (*karmātmā*), this one who wanders in transmigratory existence (*saṃsārī*) and is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*).
At that time, there is the manifestation of duality, which is characterized by the non-recognition of non-duality. (3-35)
In me, who am the true Self, the forms of "I-ness" and "this-ness" have always existed;
through the process of unraveling them, by taking recourse to the ground of the agent, [the true nature is revealed].
Once awakened, the self becomes the very form of Śiva, eternally established in its own state.
If there is no distinction, what then happens for him? To this, Śaṅkara replies:
When difference is set aside, there is the state of being the object of another creation. || 3-36 ||
p. 78) Thus, because of his Buddhahood, there is nothing whatsoever here that is distinct from the Self.

Being awakened by taking refuge in the yoga of Śiva—which unravels the bonds of karma—due to the reason of having had the heart pierced by the descent of Śiva’s power (śaktipāta), he perceives nothing as separate from the nature of Paramaśiva.

Even without further deliberation, one who possesses nothing (*akiñcana*) disregards the manifestation of duality— the locus of limited subjects such as the *pralayākala*, which consists of the egoity of the body and so forth. Such a person,
having attained stability through the reintegration into his own true nature, has acquired the supreme power of Śakti.
The meaning is that, when one has attained the great majesty appropriate for the authority of mantras, lords of mantras, and so forth,
one becomes capable of creating unprecedented creations— adorned with ever-new arrangements and delineations— without transgressing one's own will.
And this has been established by the Viśvamātṛs in their own sūtras.
When the state of one who has withdrawn from activity and one who is engaged in activity is indeed motionless,
that is the equanimity of the Buddhas— unborn and undecaying.
Thus, when differentiation is set aside, the Self possesses a single form.

Therefore, that which is the creation of another world—a novel manifestation within the process of creation—is the state of agency; such is the subjectivity of the conscious Self according to its own will. (3.36)
Regarding this, the Lord of the Gods spoke the reason concerning another creation.
The power of agency arises from its own inherent experience. (3-37)
The power (*śakti*) which resides in the instruments for the production of another creation is their capacity (*sāmarthya*);
that is established through its own inherent experience, by virtue of its reliance on an uncreated strength.
Since the capacity of the instruments arises from the power of the entry of the Self, therefore,
one who has ascended to the ground of truth can accomplish whatever effect he desires.
The Supreme Lord indeed forms such a volition;
even though all this has been stated, it is nevertheless [stated] again for the sake of clarity.

Another method is stated here, because the supernatural accomplishments (*siddhis*) are manifold: [just as] by some common power of creating the variety of the universe— such as dreams, spontaneous mental constructs, and so forth— even for a worm or similar being, there occurs the manifestation of those specific, unique things such as gardens, forests, mountains, lakes, cities, and so on.
The creative agency of objects is accessible through one's own experience. Thus, when a yogi, through intense absorption and relying upon uncontrived vigor, has ascended to that stage,
everything whatsoever he desires as an effect is accomplished according to his own volition by means of the power of his instruments.

It is being manifested. Although the means for the power to produce the manifold variety of the universe was previously mentioned, it is now restated once more in order to make known the many other varieties of the supernatural powers (*siddhis*).
Thus, one's own experience, in the form of the fourth state (*turya*), shines forth abundantly.
When, at the beginning of every creation, the Self has attained its established state,
then the Lord of the worlds speaks here with reverence regarding that [Self].
The vitalization of the three feet and so forth. || 3-38 ||
That which has the three states beginning with waking as its initial [levels] is known as the "fourth" (turya) that begins with the three states; it is designated as simultaneous fullness.

Therefore, "vitalization" (*anuprāṇana*) is the correct bestowing of one's own power upon the *bhāvas* (due to the bestowing of one's own power upon the *bhāvas*). By means of practicing the network of methods taught [previously], there arises the fourth state— the dense mass of consciousness and bliss— which vitalizes the three states beginning with waking.
When the Śiva-principle itself is perceived as perfectly complete and the establisher of all states of being, then, within the state of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*),
at the occasions of tasting and so forth regarding various desired objects such as music and the like—

The meaning is that by abiding in the state of inward-turned reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the reality of the cognizer (*boddhṛtattva*) shines forth unobstructed like a flash of lightning. || 3-8 ||
How should one act in that regard? To this, the Sūtra, which removes the darkness of the heart, says:
Just as with the stability of the mind, [the same applies] to the body, the instruments, and external objects. || 3-39 ||

The stability of the mind, whose nature has been described, is indeed its immobility— that very *cittattva* (the principle of consciousness) which, having become the mind by assuming a contracted form through its orientation toward objects of perception, [returns to its state] by following the means (*upāya*) and so forth.

Due to the restoration of the density of the innate bliss of consciousness (*svabhāva-cidānanda-ghanatā*), there is no falling away from the non-real nature even of the imagined body and so forth. For in the prior state, the entire multitude of phenomena was on an equal footing with the essence of consciousness; [only] upon turning outward...
It appears as if it has attained solidity, like a dream or a mental fantasy.

In reality, however, it is the manifestation of one's own essential nature itself that, having congealed into this or that state—appearing both externally and internally—dissolves once again and becomes the essence of consciousness (*cid-rasa*). This is the meaning.
Just as [the soul] does not fall away from its own essential nature, so it is in the case of the embodied self.

When each respective [organ] is imagined here to abide both externally and internally, the mere collection of instruments is sufficient; for that which is their abiding is indeed vitalization (prāṇana).

In this way, regarding whatever external entities (or external objects of enjoyment) one forms a conceptual construction upon, there occurs a manifestation of those very things in that same manner. (3.39)
If the outward diffusion of the multitude of objective existents occurs while they remain thus within,
why did the Consort of Girijā proclaim that?
The outward movement of that which is being carried occurs due to desire. (3.40)
That very desire which arises from the intensity of one's own power for the sake of fulfilling the immersion in action is what constitutes aspiration; therefore, it becomes fully established for him.
The outward movement of the aggregate of the instruments and so forth,
which is being carried along, is that activity proceeding with functional operation, resulting from the impulse of the impelling Self-power.
Now, that which was intended to be explained has been set forth;
however, by the logic of the crow’s eye, it has been stated again and again for the sake of the [spiritual] animal itself.
The desire for creation that exists toward all objects is sufficient;
therefore, it is said that the outward movement of the transmigrating self consists of action.
The abandonment of one's own true nature is the external multitude of sense objects;
therefore, movement and expansion therein belong to that which is being carried along.
When he is constantly carried away by objects of the senses and the like,
then the delusion known as "evil desire" unfolds within him—
even in the lower state, due to the excessive force of his own innate power.
The desire of the self, which wishes to accomplish actions such as seeing and hearing,
to bestow the power of consciousness upon the group of the intellect and the organs of action— that indeed is *abhilāṣa* (longing). By means of that very longing,
there occurs the impelling of the wheel of instruments known as the *saṃvāhya*, toward objects such as sound and touch.

The attainment of active manifestation (*pravṛttilābha*). Or rather, [the soul] is conveyed from one womb to another along with the sheaths (*kañcuka*) and so forth, which are presided over by the group of powers known as *khecarī*, *gocarī*, *dikcarī*, and *bhūcarī*.

That which is attained is the transmigrating soul, the "action-self" (karmātmā) who is like a bound beast (paśu). Due to its connection with the innate impurity (āṇavamala) called desire (abhilāṣa), which is the root of the entire mass of fetters (pāśa),
it abandons the experience of its own true nature and, out of a longing for the multitude of external objects, desires to sport therein.

There is an expansion. The meaning is that, becoming increasingly dense, it performs the function of delusion (*moha*) and, relying upon the wheel of the *bhūcarī* power (*śakti*), causes the bound souls (*paśu*) to wander. || 3-40 ||

And that which is designated as the *jīva* is the agent of action (*karmātmā*); provided that the desire for that [object] is not corrupted—[the reading "provided that the desire for that is corrupted" (*aduṣṭe tadeṣaṇe*) does not appear in other manuscripts due to a possible omission]. Ga.
Having been obtained from a manuscript, it has been compiled and arranged here.
"What would happen to the self upon the destruction of that? Then Maheśvara spoke.
The destruction of the individual soul occurs through the destruction of that valid cognition which is mounted upon it. || 3-41 ||
The prior limit is known as the ground of the perceiver when desire arises;
at that time, one who knows the ultimate truth remains awakened within it.
When, through the vigor and effort of his own power, he traverses the ground of the seer,
then that knower, having attained stable consciousness, is called a Buddha.
The cognition of the knower is his very self-awareness;
even then, there occurs the cessation of desire for the cognition that has ascended [into consciousness].
Through the destruction of that, the destruction of the one known as the "living soul" (jīva), whose nature is karma, is traditionally taught. Thus,
when there is an absence of excessive desire due to the union with a limited sense of ego, because of the experience of delusion at times—
One whose descent of power (*śaktipāta*) has arisen from the accumulation of well-performed deeds, who is intent on discerning the teaching of Śiva,

and whose consciousness has taken root in the stage of the Seer (*draṣṭṛ*), proceeds— by means of powers such as Khecarī and others— in a manner contrary to the actions of bound souls (*paśu*), starting from the coverings (*kañcuka*) up to the subtle elements (*tanmātra*).

When one relishes the essence consisting of the bliss of one's own nature— which is being manifested as the shimmering radiance of one's own consciousness, both external and internal— and thereby abandons the desire for the state of bound beings (paśu), at that very moment there occurs the cessation of this transmigrating self, the *puryaṣṭaka*. || 3-41 ||
Therefore, that which is designated as the "living soul" (jīva) is known to be bound, transmigrating, and a beast.
When the wound from the mass of nooses has been inflicted, what is the nature of the self at that time? And he said:
Then, though not yet freed from the sheath of the elements, he becomes supreme, equal to the Lord.
The five great elements (mahābhūtas) alone are the form of the fetters (pāśa), which is the sheath (kañcuka);
this sheath is to be known as a veil (āvṛti), and thus he is called "one whose sheath consists of the elements" (bhūtakañcukī).
Though previously liberated, he is indeed bound again according to the manner described before;
yet, by ascending to the stage of the All-Knowing and All-Doer (or, as in the variant reading: "the All-Knowing and the All-Doer"), he becomes another who is equal to the Lord.
This shall be so, there is no doubt in this matter; it is sufficient through one's own perfect experience.
Thus, when the impurity consisting of desire is destroyed, even while remaining in connection with a physical body—

Even while non-liberation appears, by means of the continuous rooting out of the stage of being the agent and knower of all things, he experiences his own self as the Śiva-nature— a dense mass of unsurpassed consciousness and bliss—
and thus departs from the state of the bound beast (*paśu*), though not yet due to the dissolution of the subtle body (*dehakalā*).

He becomes similar to Śiva, but not Śiva himself, because he attains that state only after the fall of the body; furthermore, his connection with the sheath of elements (bhūtakañcuka) is designated as "vital breath" (prāṇa).
How did the Blessed One Vṛṣākapi declare the sūtra in this regard?
"The connection with the vital breath is innate. (3-43)

And that which is the very connection of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) with the elemental body is to be known as innate (*nisargasiddha*), since the vital breath is composed of breath (*prāṇamaya*). [When it is for the sake of innate accomplishment, it is to be designated as consisting of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, according to the principle of the meaning already stated.]

Although, due to the realization [of the Self] as mounted upon that [state], there is necessarily the attainment of the fall of the elemental sheath (bhūtakañcuka) which is bound to it through the dissolution of the conceit of the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka),
the connection with the vital breath and the subtle body— which is the cause for the stability of that [sheath]— [remains].

It is accepted as established by nature. Indeed, consciousness itself, having first manifested as a contraction and then manifesting the diversity of the universe, resorts to the level of the subject consisting of vital breath (*prāṇa*),
and, vibrating as the world in the form of the object, manifests by its own power.

Having first forgotten its own true nature, while in the state of being alive, it accumulates meritorious and non-meritorious karma through the virtuous and non-virtuous conceptual constructions arising from itself; thus wandering through human, animal, and divine wombs appropriate to that karma, at some point...
Through the empowerment of the independent descent of power (*nirapekṣa-śaktipāta*), by ascending the sequence of the steps of the ladder of Śaiva knowledge,

those who desire the unsurpassed upper abode— even while their karmas remain, though burnt away by the fire of knowledge— continue [to experience] as long as the *prārabdha* persists, like the spinning of a wheel when the stick has been removed.
The meaning is that the experience of karma does not cease at all from the sheath of the elements bound to the vital breath (prāṇa). || 3-43 ||

Regarding this [reality] which consists of *bindu* and *nāda*, which spreads through the three paths, he has stated here that for the sake of one's own accomplishment, victory should either be achieved or not achieved. (k: for the sake of perfect accomplishment)
And here he spoke to her; (kh: and here he declared his own spiritual attainment).
By means of restraint upon the middle of the interior of the nose, what need is there here for the left, the right, or the suṣumṇā? (3.44)
The nose-tip and the dvādaśānta [twelve-finger space] beyond it constitute the locus for those whose minds are fully surrendered there;
through the practice of restraint, mastery over that is achieved, and from that, the abiding in one's own Self becomes manifest.

The "middle" here is the heart itself; therein, through the expulsion of the vital breath (prāṇa), because the functions of the mind have dissolved, the supreme arising of the Self occurs. When mastery over the vital breath is thus accomplished, what further purpose could there be in this?
In the channels of the left, right, and suṣumnā, which carry the vital breath.
Because Prāṇa is equal to Prāṇa, capable, and the bestower of all accomplishments;
this was indeed sung by Śiva within the venerable Svacchandatantra.
The vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of the vital breath; the vital breath pertains to emission (*visarga*) and filling (*āpūraṇa*).
Furthermore, the mastery of the channels of the vital breath (*prāṇanāḍī*) is said to be an incidental result.

Since the Self (*ātman*) is composed of Śiva, pure, and autonomous (*svacchanda*), therefore, upon attaining the state of the Lord (*patibhāva*)— *Note: The bracketed portion indicates a variant reading from manuscript *k* and *kh*: "is said to be an incidental result."*

For the sake of practicing the intense realization of one's own self, he points out the worship of the unstruck sound-Brahman (*anāhata-śabda-brahman*), which is the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), in the passage beginning with "within the nose. This refers to the practice of yogis whose minds are disciplined, performed at the locations where the sun of the vital breath sets, such as the "end of the twelve" (*dvādaśānta*) and other points.

Through familiarity with the practice of lying down, the conquest of the *nāḍīs* is accomplished by the dissolution of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)— which has traversed the three paths beginning with *iḍā* and has embraced the *bindu* and *nāda*. Upon the cessation of the functions of the vital breath, there arises a continuous flow of the singular realization of that [state], resulting from the resting of the mental functions within the unstruck Brahman (*anāhata-brahman*).

By virtue of becoming one with that [reality] and through the dissolution of distinctions such as the meditator and so forth, there arises the supreme Śiva of one's own self. Thus, when the goal is accomplished, for one who has attained the higher state by resting in the worship of the lower levels— such as the *uccāra* (articulation) and others taught in the *āṇava-upāya*— [the goal is reached].
The intention of the collection of verses [is expressed as follows]: "Because there is no dependence on other subsequent words. || 3-44 ||

Thus, in these three chapters, it was spoken by the All-pervading One (vibhu)—[variant k: "in this chapter here also by the Non-all-pervading one"; variant kh: "enlightened by the All-pervading one"].
And regarding that, he states the established conclusion: "The binding through the application of skillful means shall result once again in a complete merging. (3.45)
In this manner, according to the view thus stated, this entire world is the manifestation of His will;
therefore, everything belongs to the All-pervasive Lord, while the individual soul is distinct due to the power of His illusory energy (*māyā-śakti*).
He recognized himself once again through the instruction according to the method previously described.
Through the removal of turbidity, there occurs a merging with the Lord;
for when he has attained non-separateness from the Supreme Lord, [merging] with the Lord takes place.
Thus, he becomes Śiva, whose bliss is entirely full and undifferentiated.
(In this way, the essence of the Śaiva system as previously described is here indicated in brief;
furthermore, it is Paramaśiva himself, whose nature is supreme consciousness and the unsurpassed, who, through the progression of the power of his own will, [manifests the universe].)

Having unfolded the sprouts of Śiva, Śakti, and so forth, he presides over the pure path (*śuddhādhvan*). While remaining on this much of the path, he does not deviate from his own nature as a dense mass of consciousness; however, on the lower path, by means of the intention to display a play consisting of the forgetting of his true nature, there arises the state of being a subject under *māyā*.

Resting within me, he performs the universal drama; he alone, having manifested the nature of knowledge and action through the descent of the most intense power (*tīvratama-śaktipāta*), his own latent powers and splendors being withdrawn, submerges the state of the individual knower (*kṣetrajña*) according to the path of Śaiva knowledge, and upon the purification of impurities, [attains] perfect consciousness and bliss.
Having emerged into the state of the dense, unsurpassed, and supreme Śiva, he returns to his own natural state; thus [ends the section]. || 3-45 ||
Thus, this excellent Sūtravārtika has been correctly described in brief by three hundred and ninety verses.
Thus,

these three chapters, which have issued from the mouth of Śiva, have now been slightly unveiled by me for the sake of the accomplishment of those with excellent intelligence; they are well-constructed and easy to grasp.
Having reflected upon this, may it be fully resorted to by people who have abandoned envy and who perceive virtues; therein, may it abundantly bestow both spiritual accomplishment and liberation.
Thus ends the third chapter, titled "The Vibration of the Empowerment," in the *Śivasūtravārtika* composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Bhāskara, son of the illustrious Kashmiri teacher Bhaṭṭa Divākara. || 3 ||
And this work, titled Śivasūtravārtika, is completed.
May it be offered unto the venerable Śiva.
